Headline: Tragedy on road 'always with you'
Full Text:
It's six years this Easter Sunday since Belinda Dowell's son Brandon died on an "ordinary drive" near Kangaroo Ground.

    As Victoria Police launches its biggest road safety blitz of the year, she's begging drivers: Don't let another family live with this pain.

    Operation Nexus will be a highly visible police presence on the state's roads over the Easter long weekend.

    The operation will deploy all available resources, from general duties to highway patrol and specialist road units.

    Acting Assistant Commissioner Justin Goldsmith said police wanted every person to make it home safely to their loved ones this Easter.

    "We know this is a weekend that attracts significant travel across the state, so we won't be taking any chances, and neither should you," he said.

    Ms Dowell's eldest son Brandon lost control of his vehicle between Wattle Glen and Kangaroo Ground, northeast of Melbourne, just before Easter 2020. The 27-year-old died while trapped in his car.

    "In a single moment on an ordinary drive, our family was torn apart," Ms Dowell said.

    "We went home without Brandon. And we've been living with that loss every single day since.

    "That's what road trauma does. It doesn't just happen in that moment on the road; it follows you home. It sits at your dinner table. It's there at every birthday, every Christmas, every Easter."

    Ms Dowell is urging everyone hitting the road this Easter break to take extra care.

    "This coming Sunday, Easter Sunday, marks six years (since Brandon's death), so please, slow down," she said.

    "Stay focused, don't take risks.

    "Because when something goes wrong on the road, it's not just a crash. It's a family ... like ours ... left to live with it forever."

    Operation Nexus begins at 12.01am on Thursday and wraps up at 11.59pm on Monday.

Bass Coast Highway Patrol is investigating and anyone with dashcam footage is asked to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

Headline: Police charge 13yo girl after alleged antisemitic rampage in Melbourne
Full Text:
A 13-year-old girl has been charged over a spree of motor vehicle crimes in Melbourne's south-east over the past week. ABC News: Che Chorley

    A 13-year-old girl has been charged with dozens of offences, including multiple car thefts and hit-and-run incidents.

    

    The teenager is also accused of shouting antisemitic remarks and swerving a car towards a Jewish family in Melbourne's south-east.

    

    The girl was arrested on Tuesday morning and remanded to appear at a children's court.

    

    A 13-year-old girl has been charged with 52 offences after allegedly shouting antisemitic remarks at members of Melbourne's Jewish community and driving a stolen car erratically towards them.

    

    Police say a black Hyundai sedan was stolen from a gym in Caulfield in Melbourne's south-east, and then used across multiple days last week to commit crimes in Hampton, Ripponlea and Caulfield.

    

    The teenage girl is accused of driving the car as its passengers shouted offensive, antisemitic remarks and threw eggs at pedestrians.

    

    The girl is also accused of swerving the car towards a group of people from the Jewish community in Ripponlea as they crossed a road.

    

    Investigators say the same 13-year-old was involved in an alleged hit-and-run in Brighton on Monday night.

    

    Police say a cyclist was riding along St Kilda Street when an occupant of a stolen silver SUV attempted to hit the bike with the passenger door.

    

    The SUV then crashed into the rear of the bike before fleeing the scene.

    

    The cyclist, a 45-year-old Brighton man, was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

    

    The rampage continued into the early hours of Tuesday morning, when teenagers in a stolen white Volkswagen Golf rammed into the back of an e-scooter in Elwood just after midnight.

    

    The e-scooter's riders both fell as it crashed into a parked vehicle, and the offenders again fled the scene.

    

    Police say the stolen Volkswagen was later seen on Beach Road in Black Rock, and led officers on a chase across the Eastlink, Princes Highway and the Monash Freeway before being stopped.

    

    The three female occupants were arrested at the scene and taken into custody.

    

    Police have charged the 13-year-old with dozens of offences, including:

    

    reckless conduct endanger serious injury

    

    multiple counts of theft

    

    multiple counts of theft of motor vehicle

    

    burglary

    

    handle stolen goods

    

    threaten physical harm or property damage on ground of a protected attribute

    

    She was remanded to appear at a children's court.

    

    A 16-year-old girl and a 13-year-old girl were also arrested and charged with theft of motor vehicle and handle stolen goods and were bailed to appear at a children's court at a later date.

    

    Victoria Police say investigations into the series of incidents are ongoing and urge anyone who witnessed the incidents, with dashcam or CCTV footage to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

Headline: Traffic chaos erupts, biker fighting for life after horror crash on major Victorian freeway
Full Text:
A motorcyclist is fighting for life after a horror crash along a major Victorian freeway, with multiple lanes closed.

    A biker is fighting for life after a horror crash shut down a key section of a major Victorian highway, sparking traffic chaos.

    

    Emergency services, including an air ambulance, are at the scene of a crash on the Monash Freeway at Endeavour Hills, on the edge of Melbourne.

    

    The freeway is currently closed to outbound traffic between Heatherton Rd and Belgrave-Hallam Rd, with motorists being diverted through Dandenong South.

    

    A Victoria Police spokesman said: "Emergency services responded to a collision in Endeavour Hills on Tuesday.

    

    "It is believed two cars and a motorcycle collided on the Monash Freeway near Heatherton Rd just after 3.30pm.

    

    "The motorcyclist will be flown to hospital in a critical condition.

    

    "The drivers of the cars were not injured and stopped at the scene to assist. The exact cause of the collision is being investigated."

    

    An Ambulance Victoria spokesman confirmed that an air ambulance crew is on scene, along with advance life support and intensive care support.

    

    The spokesman said: "Ambulance Victoria was called to an incident in the Endeavour Hills at around 2.50pm today."

    

    "A specialist air ambulance helicopter crew, advanced life support and mobile intensive care ambulance paramedic crews attended the scene.

    

    "One patient is being transported to the Royal Melbourne Hospital."

Headline: Local roads boost in South Gippsland Shire
Full Text:
WITH funding secured for seven street projects across South Gippsland Shire, community members are being asked their views, with works planned for Leongatha, Foster, Loch, Sandy Point, Korumburra and Venus Bay.

    South Gippsland Shire Council secured $2 million of funding from the Transport Accident Commission (TAC) to help make local streets safer, directing the money to key locations that have been identified for safety upgrades.

    The overall project includes the installation of speed cushions, mini roundabouts, pedestrian crossings, and reduced speed limits in busy areas, council stating that the intention is to improve safety and accessibility for drivers, cyclists and pedestrians.

    An interactive map related to each planned project and a description of why it is considered necessary and what is involved are available by visiting southgippsland.vic. gov.au and selecting 'Safe Local Roads and Streets'.

    Leongatha: Two projects are planned for Leongatha.

    One involves the installation of mini roundabouts along Peart Street and its continuation Bruce Street at the intersections of Allison, Bellingham, Smith and Church Streets.

    These roundabouts will include pedestrian crossings.

    Council notes that Peart/ Bruce Street is an important thoroughfare to reach Leongatha's shopping area, with the locations selected for mini roundabouts being some of the highest volume intersections in South Gippsland.

    The other planned Leongatha project is intended to significantly improve safety for children walking to the town's schools.

    It involves the installation of road cushions along MacDonald Street to encourage drivers to slow down, along with the creation of a raised pedestrian crossing near the Ogilvy Street intersection, and filling in the footpath gaps on the east side of MacDonald Street.

    A short portion of MacDonald Street will be narrowed to accommodate the new footpath section.

    Foster: While Foster's Main Street was recently upgraded through council's streetscape project for the town, there are opportunities to make further improvements in the way Foster's traffic operates, council states.

    The project entails upgraded pedestrian crossings on Main Street throughout the shopping centre, supported by road cushions/ raised platforms to manage vehicle speeds.

    Raised crossings will be constructed at the intersection of Main and Station Streets, between the Exchange Hotel and IGA, as well as the existing crossing near Pearl Park.

    Loch: Loch will receive a variety of works to encourage safer travel within the town, ensuring drivers are aware they are entering residential areas.

    Pedestrian crossings will be created around the intersections of Victoria Road with Roy, Clarence and Smith Streets, with the Smith Street intersection to be converted into a mini roundabout to help reduce the speed of vehicles entering the parking area at the shops.

    A raised pedestrian crossing will be introduced on Victoria Road near Loch Primary School, making it safer for children walking to school or being dropped off or picked up.

    Road cushions will be placed at regular intervals in Clarence Street to reinforce the 50km/h speed limit.

    "Victoria Road will have its speed limit reduced to 40km/h through the builtup area to support the treatments," council states.

    Sandy Point: Sandy Point community members have called for more support in managing vehicle speeds to boost safety for those walking around town.

    The approach taken in the announced project plan is the introduction of mini roundabouts that will be supported by road cushions to promote safe vehicle entry speeds without impeding walkers or cyclists.

    There will be greater separation of vehicles and pedestrians at key locations near the main parking area, along with an upgraded pedestrian crossing between the shops and the main beach entry.

    The entry speed limit on Telopea Drive will be reduced from 80km/h to 50km/h, before the current 40km/h speed limit through town.

    Korumburra: In Korumburra, feedback on the need for improved safety on Princes Street for those attending St Joseph's Primary School, Karmai Community Centre, and Korumburra Primary School has driven planning that will entail raised pedestrian crossings at key locations along Princes Street.

    That includes the roundabout intersection with Bridge Street and Shellcot Road.

    The school crossings on Princes Street and Bridge Street will be supported with road cushions, but won't be changed into fulltime zebra crossings, with supervisors to continue helping children cross at school start and finish times.

    Venus Bay: A 2025 petition containing 339 signatures called on South Gippsland Shire Council to develop speed treatments in Venus Bay, with council now seizing the opportunity to address concerns of high vehicle speeds through the town.

    Road cushions will be installed through Lees Road and Canterbury Road, through all three Venus Bay estates, as well as providing gateway treatments to either end of the 'Mad Mile', to reinforce to drivers they are entering residential areas.

    The cushions are intended to discourage drivers from exceeding the 50km/h limit, while still allowing them to travel comfortably at that speed.

    As well as boosting pedestrian safety, the changes in Venus Bay will benefit local wildlife.

Headline: ARRESTS MADE Arrests made in hoon, burglary investigation
Full Text:
Maryborough police arrested two men earlier this month allegedly linked to a burglary at Maryborough Golf Club and recent hoon activity. Central Goldfields Highway Patrol Sergeant Paul Martin said police remained focused on dangerous driving. 310326 44 Story, Page 4.

    SAM MCNEILL An overlapping police investigation into hoon driving around Maryborough and a burglary at the town's golf club has resulted in two arrests earlier in March.

    Maryborough Police executed three search warrants on Tuesday, March 17, arresting two males.

    The investigation related to a burglary at the Maryborough Golf Club on February 20, where a safe and tens of thousands of dollars was stolen, and recent hoon driving activity around Maryborough.

    Local police allege the two incidents are linked.

    The investigation involved members from the Central Goldfields Crime Investigation Unit, Central Goldfields Highway Patrol and uniform officers.

    Detectives seized two motor vehicles and one motorcycle connected to the alleged offences.

    A 30-year-old male from Maryborough has been charged with numerous offences including trafficking drugs, dangerous driving while pursued by police and property offences.

    He was remanded in custody to appear at the Bendigo Magistrates Court on April 30, 2026.

    A 31-year-old Maryborough man was charged with drug possession offences and bailed to the Maryborough Magistrates Court on May 14, 2026.

    Maryborough Police said enquiries are ongoing.

    Maryborough Golf Club general manager Bonaventure Tai said the burglary had a significant impact on the business.

    Among what was stolen was operational equipment, Mr Tai said, which meant he closed the gaming section due to staff safety concerns.

    Around a month before the burglary, he said there was another break in at the business but nothing was stolen.

    "It certainly alerted us to upgrade our security ... but unfortunately they got in before I got the new processes in place," he said.

    Since February's burglary, however, he said his team and the community have been incredibly supportive.

    "I put my hand on my heart the community was as upset as I was that this had happened," he said.

    "The support of the community has been overwhelming."

    Central Goldfields Highway Patrol are continuing their investigation into hoon driving in the Maryborough area.

    "We know that precursors to hoon driving activity often begins with illegally modified and unroadworthy vehicles which remains a current focus of police," Maryborough Police said in a statement.

    Maryborough Police warned those found using an unroadworthy vehicle can be issued with a vehicle defect notice, as well as an on the spot fine of $814, and those caught hoon driving can expect police will make an application to have the vehicle impounded for 30 days at "significant cost".

    Police urge the community to report incidents of hoon and dangerous driving via Crime Stopper at crimestoppersvic.com.au, by calling 1300 333 000, or by contacting local police.

Headline: Wollert man loses licence
Full Text:
A Wollert man has lost his licence allegedly over multiple offences.

    He was allegedly caught driving over double the speed limit, under the influence of alcohol and without his P-plates in Lalor.

    Greensborough Highway Patrol officers were conducting speed checks on the Hume Freeway when they spotted the black BMW sedan speeding just before 2am on Sunday, March 22.

    The vehicle was allegedly detected travelling at 205km/h in a 100km/h zone northbound between the Metropolitan Ring Road and Cooper Street.

    Officers intercepted the vehicle on Cooper Street, where they found the driver had failed to display his P-plates.

    Police did an evidentiary breath test that returned an alleged reading of .021.

    The 22-year-old Wollert man was arrested and immediately lost his licence.

    He was charged with offences including reckless conduct endangering life, driving at dangerous speed, exceeding prescribed concentration of alcohol within three hours breath test, and driving without P-plates.

    He was bailed to appear at Heidelberg Magistrates' Court on June 10.

Headline: Drunk Uber Eats driver, Masood Safdary, pleads guilty to drunk driving offences
Full Text:
A drunk Uber Eats driver failed to obey police despite the lights and siren after they saw him using his phone. When they did finally get him to pull over he blew almost four times the legal limit.

    An Uber Eats driver won't be doing any deliveries for a while after he was busted behind the wheel while almost four times the legal limit, telling a court he was "new in Australia".

    

    Masood Safdary, 36, appeared in the Dandenong Magistrates' Court on Tuesday where he pleaded guilty to drink-driving and using his phone

    

    In January 2025, Safdary was spotted by police using his phone, which was mounted on the right side of his dashboard, driving slowly along Power Rd, Doveton, about midnight.

    

    When police activated their lights and sirens to alert Safdary to pull over he failed to obey and they had to drive alongside him to to get his attention.

    

    A breath test returned a reading of 0.182 — almost four times the legal limit

    

    Police issued Safdary an immediate 12-month driving ban.

    

    The court also heard that Safdary's licence was suspended by a different court in February this year on separate matters until September 19, 2027.

    

    On Tuesday, while representing himself, Safdary told the court he was unemployed as he could not work as an Uber Eats driver without his licence.

    

    He told the court he had worked as an Uber Eats driver for three months prior to being caught.

    

    Safdary — born in Afghanistan — migrated to Australia from India where he had lived for 10 years.

    

    "I really apologise for my behaviour, I was new in Australia," he said.

    

    Magistrate Luisa Bazzani told Safdary that he was "nearly four-times the legal limit".

    

    "You could kill someone," she said.

    

    "I'm sick and tired of hearing every excuse under the sun why people do this.

    

    "Do not think having your licence is a right; it is a privilege."

    

    He was fined $1500 without conviction and his licence was disqualified for 20 months from January 17, 2025.

Headline: Customs loophole fuels flood of illegal high-speed e-bikes onto Melbourne streets
Full Text:
A simple questionnaire is allowing thousands of illegal e-bikes to hit Melbourne's streets, as retailers show riders sneaky tactics to avoid speed restrictions and fines.

    A simple questionnaire when filling out a customs form allows thousands of to be imported into Melbourne with fatal consequences.

    

    Scores of the dodgy delivery bikes are shipped into Melbourne by importers who declare the bikes are "not for road use" when signing customs forms.

    

    That allows the bikes to be shipped in with little scrutiny from border officials who are more focused on preventing illicit drugs and tobacco from entering the country.

    

    The bikes are then moved to suburban stockists who sell them to students and young people trying to make cash delivering food.

    

    "The demand for 'not for road use' e-bikes is significant," Beckham Liu, PhD candidate at UNSW, said.

    

    The Herald Sun can reveal e-bike retailers have also told customers how to evade legal speed and power limits — while also outlining how riders can avoid

    

    Federal law states that the several forms of e-bikes should not exceed 25km/h or 250 watts.

    

    But one customer, who relayed their conversation with an e-bike salesperson, said the Melbourne company held little concerns about the safety and legality of their products.

    

    "So that goes up to 25 (km/h), yeah, but when you change the gear, the real speed is 40, 45 (km/h) plus," the sales member working at the inner-city store said.

    

    "We (don't) get in trouble because they request. When the customer requests, we can do it. Okay. But it's under their responsibility, not our company.

    

    "If they want, they just pay, they sign, and they get it."

    

    The loophole which allows e-bikes to be shipped into the country also continues to be exploited by overseas manufacturers.

    

    Official customs guidelines state that "vehicles that are not road vehicles must not be supplied to the market or sold to another person or business for use in transport on public roads".

    

    Several industry figures told the Herald Sun that law is being blatantly ignored.

    

    "They have covered their legal liability by stating in fine print 'for private property use only' — placing the legal obligation for road riding an illegal motorcycle on the rider," another industry source said.

    

    Coroner Audrey Jamieson agreed.

    

    "According to the CPU (Coroners Prevention Unit), there is ample evidence that Australian e-bicycle retailers import and sell vehicles that would be too powerful to be classified as e-bicycles in some jurisdictions, such as Victoria," Coroner Jamieson said during an inquest last year.

    

    "In doing so, retailers can advertise vehicles as for 'off road' or disengage certain features to reduce their maximum speed – which can be easily re-engaged by consumers."

    

    Mr Liu, who recently interviewed 100 food delivery drivers, said the riders overwhelming chose to travel on the illegal bikes as it sped up the delivery process.

    

    "Several riders mentioned using both legal and illegal vehicles but ultimately chose the illegal ones," he added.

    

    "One interviewee (said) faster deliveries means more money."

    

    Food delivery riders are often seen travelling in the wrong direction, driving through red lights and defying the legal speed and power limits.

    

    One man was filmed driving in the wrong direction along the Tullamarine Freeway on Saturday, riding in the emergency lane against cars and trucks travelling at least 80km/h.

    

    A number of food delivery drivers have been killed on the state's roads in recent years but day-to-day enforcement remains difficult for authorities.

    

    Victoria Police have conducted several targeted operations on e-bike riders but they are difficult to track as the bikes are not registered.

Headline: NDIS rorters to face jail time
Full Text:
The Senate has passed new laws under which dodgy National Disability Insurance Scheme providers could be jailed for years and fined millions amid widespread reports of rorting.

    The legislation passed on Tuesday targets serious misconduct in the NDIS, threatening up to five years' jail time for people who violate a banning order and two years for anyone providing support without being properly registered.

    The Bill must now pass the House of Representatives, where Labor holds a mammoth majority.

    NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister said the NDIS "is meant to be a disability support scheme, not a get-rich-quick scheme".

    "If you are banned from the NDIS, but then choose to contravene that banning order, then you do not belong in the disability sector, you belong in prison," Senator McAllister said.

    "If you think you can get rich quick and cut corners by operating without registration when it is needed then you are engaging in predatory and dangerous behaviour and you also belong in prison.

    "And if you think you can get away with shonky marketing, which tricks NDIS participants into misusing their funding, tricks investors into disability housing scams, or promotes fake deals that tell participants they can use their plans to fund holidays then we will fine you $400,000," she said.

    NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commissioner Louise Glanville said: "These new laws will support the NDIS Commission to take more effective action to prevent harm and improve quality across the sector."

Headline: 'High reward, high risk'
Full Text:
The reality behind our SDA investment surge

    THE Specialist Disability Accommodation (SDA) market grew sharply to more than $600 million, attracting property investors to build, including in Ballarat.

    The latest report shows total SDA support rose 43 per cent over two years to $626 million, with 15,925 participants.

    Currently, Ballarat has 307 participants with SDA funding, with 264 actively using it and 43 eligible but not yet accessing the support.

    The average SDA support is about $34,200 per person per year.

    The SDA housing market in Ballarat is estimated to be worth about $10.5 million in 2026.

    Despite strong market growth, Ballarat SDA provider ELJET Property Group owners Emily Hines and Jessica Hughes said they would not recommend further builds unless the homes were purpose-built.

    "The return on an SDA versus a rental property is much higher," Ms Hines said.

    "I think in the last five years, there has been a huge oversupply of SDA homes, not just in Ballarat.

    "It's been saturated, with people just building and building."

    According to the SDA Finder, the Gold Rush city currently has 57 properties listed, providing accommodation for about 120 residents, with 105 rooms currently vacant. Continued - page 7 Investment returns 'not a guarantee'

    From page 1 "Now in Ballarat, I wouldn't just build an SDA home and hope to fill it, because there simply isn't the participant base anymore," Ms Hines said.

    "Most people are already living in suitable accommodation, and SDA funding is becoming increasingly difficult to obtain."

    SDA homes are often marketed as high-yield investment opportunities, delivering annual returns as high as 12 per cent, enticing investors with the promise of strong, stable income.

    Ms Hughes said investors often overlooked a key condition: returns only begin once rooms are occupied, and achieving the projected maximum return was often challenging.

    "They're probably looking at that and thinking, 'This is the best option for achieving the highest return on an investment property', without really looking into the background."

    An National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIA) spokesperson told The Courier in a statement the NDIA does not build, own or commission SDA.

    "The upfront investment of buying or building SDA dwellings comes from the owner or investor. The NDIA does not guarantee investment returns."

    Ms Hines said she received a phone call three or four weeks ago from a mother whose son had invested in an SDA build in Winter Valley about 18 months earlier, but the property had remained vacant ever since.

    "It was built as a two-resident, robust and improved liveability design. You could tell it was built to maximise the amount of return that that person could get. But to have a participant that has two-resident funding in the first place is near impossible to find.

    "It's high reward, but it's high risk." Born and raised in Ballarat, Ms Hines said SDA should not be viewed purely as an investment, but as an opportunity to deliver stable housing for people who need support.

    Ms Hines said she and her sister, Ms Hughes, launched their SDA home business in 2020 after working on the support side with their family.

    "It was in the transition time. We found that many providers, including SDA providers, were not based in Ballarat, so residents often had to contact someone in Melbourne or elsewhere. Their SDA housing was tied to their support services, so to live in a particular property with that provider, you also had to use their supports. We wanted to create an opportunity to have that completely separate."

    The white weatherboard home with a pink door was one of the projects undertaken by Ms Hines and Ms Hughes.

    "From the start, we build homes participants want to live in," Ms Hines said.

    "The pink door was chosen by the two girls. They came from former models of SDA, like government-funded group homes.

    "They wanted to move out of that and into a place that felt like home."

    Ms Hines said group homes were often very clinical, with cold lino floors and hospital-style bathrooms.

    "It's fit for purpose as far as nursing requirements, but it doesn't feel like a home."

    Ms Hughes said they often found participants' support funding did not align with how they wanted to live.

    And in the next few years, they would like to focus efforts on assisting participants through the SDA application process.

    Ms Hines said they believed that stable, secure, functional housing was the foundation for anyone to live a quality life.

    "We see people less reliant on supports, independently accessing the community, creating social connections, entering the workforce ... all of which is possible due to feeling secure and empowered in their SDA home," she said.

    It's been saturated, with people just building and building Emily Hines

    I wouldn't just build an SDA home and hope to fill it, because there simply isn't the participant base anymore

Headline: Fuel crisis puts pressure on workers, business, as calls to work from home reignite
Full Text:
Rebecca Grey is a sole trader occupational therapist in Perth who says fuel costs are impacting her growing business. ABC News: Keane Naughton

    The fuel crisis is putting pressure on workers who rely on car travel and those that meet with vulnerable clients, with fresh calls for front-line support staff to be exempt from possible fuel rationing mandates.

    

    There are also renewed calls for more employees to work from home, though experts say the crisis has not yet reached "tipping point".

    

    It comes after the federal government introduced a national fuel security plan on Monday and announced it would halve the fuel excise for three months, starting on Wednesday.

    

    As a result, petrol prices will reduce by 26.3 centre per litre, a saving of approximately $19 for a 65-litre tank.

    

    The government announced it will halve the fuel excise for three months, passing savings onto consumers. ABC News: Chris Taylor

    

    Federal treasurer Jim Chalmers said people in regional and rural Australia "were front of mind" when making the decision about the fuel excise.

    

    "One of the reasons why we landed on this approach to providing more cost-of-living relief in what we're announcing is because for people who unavoidably have to drive longer distances, the benefit will be greater," he said on Monday.

    

    However, economists said while there was a short-term benefit, the underlying factors that drove up the price of fuel still remained.

    

    "In three months, unless the measure is extended, we will observe a jump up in the price of fuel," Professor of Economics, Fabrizio Carmignani, said.

    

    "Also, it's a measure that will benefit consumers depending on the level of consumption of fuel, and we know that typically in this situation, it's a measure that is not necessarily targeted at the more vulnerable houses."

    

   Push for WFH directive

     The oil crisis has fundamentally shifted the work-from-home (WFH) debate from a workplace culture issue to a practical way for workers to save money at the bowser and to conserve fuel stocks.

    

    The International Energy Agency's call to limit travel and encourage remote working has given unions fresh ammunition, particularly for office-based and finance sector workers who proved during the pandemic they could work productively from home.

    

    Wesfarmers, whose brands include Bunnings, Kmart, Target, Officeworks and Priceline, confirmed it had temporarily suspended non-essential travel for its corporate team members and discouraged flights.

    

    The rising cost of fuel is impacting employees who rely on vehicles for their work. ABC News: Chris Taylor

    

    For those with long commutes, living regionally, or with limited public transport, working from home is being framed less as a lifestyle preference and more as an economic necessity.

    

    Aged care provider, Prestige InHome Care, will now allow frontline staff to work from home "where possible," as a direct measure to ease costs for workers.

    

    "The cost of travel to and from work has gone up exponentially," chief executive Mark O'Brien said.

    

    "We are confident that our organisation can continue to deliver our services working remote."

    

    The company has also boosted rebates for kilometres travelled by frontline carers and introduced roster changes to reduce excess travel.

    

    Professor Fabrizio Carmignani says it's a "lose-lose" situation for the government at the moment. ABC News: Lucas Hill

    

    Pulling in the opposite direction is a growing resistance from some business leaders and economists who warn that Australia is not yet at "tipping point".

    

    "The shortages we are seeing are not so critical at the moment to justify a general directive to work from home," Professor Carmignani said.

    

    "If we were to be in a situation where you go to the service station and pumps are shut down, or the moment when we see that there are very long lines, [or] the shortage is such that we need to ration the supply of fuel … that definitely could be a point where we might want to consider generalised directives.

    

    "For some individuals, it might make sense already now to discuss arrangements with their employers."

    

    Professor Fabrizio said even though it might seem "reactive", it was currently a "lose-lose" situation for the government no matter what direction it took.

    

    "There is no magic wand,"

    

    he said.

    

    "We don't want to put in place directives that damage the economy beyond what is necessary based on the information that we have today."

    

    Internationally, governments are responding to the tightening fuel supply with a mix of behavioural and workplace measures.

    

    The Philippines has floated a four-day working week, Thailand has promoted remote work and limits on air-conditioning use while driving, while Vietnam has urged citizens to reduce travel altogether.

    

    Unlike COVID, many workers — particularly in health, disability, cleaning, transport and trades — cannot work remotely at all, and work from home directives risks entrenching inequity between office professionals and frontline workers.

    

    Employers are also wary of productivity losses and coordination challenges and the long- term hollowing out of CBDs.

    

   Concerns carers unable to afford fuel

     Rebecca Grey is a sole trader occupational therapist based in Perth's southern suburbs, who works with clients across homes, schools and workplaces.

    

    She said driving an older petrol car meant fuel costs were having a huge impact on her new business.

    

    "My practice involves direct, face-to-face therapy, which is a clinical necessity for the type of work I do," she said.

    

    "I'm in the early stages of building my practice, so my caseload is still growing. Being flexible about where I travel is essential right now, but this crisis makes that much harder."

    

    Ms Grey is a single parent with a mortgage, so any business costs come out of her pocket before she earns anything. ABC News: Keana Naughton

    

    She said there is no telehealth substitute for the therapy and assessments she undertakes and is worried about possible fuel shortages.

    

    "If there's no fuel at the petrol station, I can't see clients,"

    

    she said.

    

    Angus McFarland, NSW/ACT secretary of the Australian Services Union said it was being "inundated" with calls from NDIS workers who cannot afford fuel.

    

    The ASU has welcomed the halving of the fuel excise, which will help ease cost-of-living pressures.

    

    "We're calling on the federal government to provide [further] fuel relief for essential disability support workers in the NDIS and we're also calling on them to make sure that community and care workers are deemed essential workers in the event that at some point there is a rationing system that comes in," he said.

    

   Businesses step in to offer travel relief

     A Melbourne-based cleaning company, that has been in operation for 25 years, said its diverse workforce, many who are single parents or students, were struggling to make ends meet.

    

    "Many staff are in transitional phases of their lives really [with] obvious pressures," Liz Talevski said.

    

    Managing Director Liz Talevski says the company is making small, practical measures now to help staff. ABC News: Patrick Stone

    

    The M1 Cleaning Group has implemented practical measures to help staff with rising costs, including vouchers for fuel and transport, smarter rostering to reduce split shifts and carpooling and car sharing with company vehicles.

    

    "Our workers already commute big distances with their daily activities, so any way we can help with that is a positive thing for everyone," she said.

    

    We don't really know what's ahead of us so practical measures, small changes, [make a] huge impact.

    

    Pedro Soto (left) and Yuliana Echeverry (right) have benefited from fuel and public transport vouchers from their employer. ABC News: Patrick Stone

    

    Pedro Soto, who works for the company, said he made cuts to travelling or used more public transport due to the price hikes.

    

    "It's been very difficult," he said.

    

    "The price has increased a lot … I have to cut some travelling, I have to use more public transport.

    

    "[The vouchers] make a very, very big difference for myself and for staff."

Headline: Disability agency adds nearly 2,000 new employees while trying to rein in costs
Full Text:
The agency that runs the NDIS expanded its workforce by nearly 2,000 positions in 2025. AAP: Mick Tsikas

    The NDIA hired almost 2,000 new staff last year, accounting for nearly 70 per cent of all new hires to the public service.

    

    It comes as the government works to rein in the cost of the NDIS, which is expected to cost $50 billion this financial year

    

    The NDIA said the influx of staff will deliver better outcomes for participants and reduce wait times.

    

    The agency that runs the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) has defended hiring nearly 2,000 new employees last year despite major changes being rolled out to rein in the program's cost.

    

    The NDIA grew its workforce by 1,925 new positions in 2025, accounting for nearly 70 per cent of all new hires to the Commonwealth public service last year.

    

    Data published by the Australian Public Service Commission showed overall 2,782 jobs were added to the APS in 2025, expanding the workforce by 1.44 per cent.

    

    The National Disability Insurance Agency's (NDIA) staff numbers expanded by 21 per cent over the same time.

    

    A spokesperson for the NDIA said the agency had bolstered frontline staff in the last year to ensure it delivered better outcomes for participants, reduced wait times and provided a better overall experience.

    

    As part of the flurry of hiring, more than 400 new executive level employees joined the agency's ranks.

    

    The NDIA went from employing 9,127 staff at the end of 2024 to having 11,052 people on its payroll at the end of 2025.

    

    No other government department or agency added more new staff in 2025 than the NDIA.

    

    Do you work for the NDIA or have you previously? Tell us more and contact specialist.team@abc.net.au

    

    George Taleporos, chair of Every Australian Counts, the grassroots movement that pushed for the establishment of the NDIS, said participants and their families would have mixed feelings about the additional staff.

    

    "(We) support increased staffing if it leads to faster response times, more effective decision-making, better communication, and a more responsive experience for participants," he said.

    

   Structural change

     The federal government is implementing a major reset of disability support, driven by cost cutting and pressure to rein in the growth of the NDIS, which is expected to cost $50 billion this financial year and $60 billion by 2030.

    

    While its annual growth has halved in recent years to 10.3 per cent, the government wants to see that fall even further to around 6 per cent.

    

    Cost cutting and an expanding workforce were not necessarily contradictory, said economist Pelin Akyol from economics think tank, the e61 Institute.

    

    "Reforming a scheme the size of the National Disability Insurance Scheme often requires up-front administrative investment," Ms Akyol said.

    

    She said the agency may have added additional planners to assess participants under the new planning framework.

    

    Later this year, the NDIA is introducing a new way of assessing participants' plans that will rely less on reports from medical practitioners and more on interviews with assessors within the agency.

    

    Ms Akyol also said tighter regulations for some disability service providers coming into effect in July could require higher staff numbers.

    

    The number of participants on the NDIS has grown to over 760,000. ABC News: Nicole Mills

    

    Dr Taleporos said increasing staff numbers alone did not guarantee better outcomes for participants.

    

    "We don't want a larger bureaucracy, with more rules and restrictions on participants," he said.

    

    "The agency exists to serve people with disability and our families, not to consume a growing share of NDIS resources without clear improvements in participant experience and outcomes."

    

    The number of participants on the NDIS has grown from nearly 400,000 in 2019-2020 to more than 760,000 at the end of last year.

    

    Ms Akyol said adding nearly 2,000 staff members was a significant expansion of the workforce and it might help participants get the help they need.

    

   Tribunal workforce swells

     The Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) also grew significantly, increasing its workforce by 33.45 per cent.

    

    The ART replaced the Administrative Appeals Tribunal in October 2024 as the body which reviews decisions made by government agencies, departments and ministers.

    

    NDIS matters are the fastest growing caseload for the ART.

    

    Data for the current financial year shows 10 per cent of matters lodged with the tribunal relate to the NDIS, up from 6 per cent the previous year.

    

    The NDIA spent $60 million on external legal firms in 2024-25 to fight participants appealing cuts to their plans.

    

    Alongside cuts to plans, Dr Taleporos said participants and their families had reported less flexibility and control over how they used their funding.

    

    "If more staff are needed to make the agency work better for participants then we welcome this, but it is essential that this doesn't lead to cuts to our supports or restrictions on how we live our lives," he said.

    

    The agency that runs the NDIS is under pressure to reduce the cost of the scheme. 7.30 Report

    

    Of the new employees that started at the NDIA last year, 450 were APS level 3-4. These junior staff members are customer-facing, work under substantial supervision and deal with straightforward enquiries.

    

    More than 1,000 were APS level 5-6, which involves solving difficult problems, managing complex customer relationships and making sensitive decisions.

    

    A further 400 executive level roles were added. In these positions, staff perform leadership roles with a considerable degree of independence.

    

    In 2024, the NDIA added 2,313 new jobs as its staff numbers grew by 34 per cent.

    

    The NDIA now has 10,671 ongoing employees, an increase of 1,939 positions since 2024.

    

    Just over 380 staff at the agency are now employed on an on-ongoing basis, down from 395 in 2024.

    

    The biggest employers in the federal public service at the end of last year were Services Australia, the Tax Office, Defence and Home Affairs.

Headline: Australian schools are getting $5bn a year in disability funding – search the list and get expert tips on accessing support for your child
Full Text:
Up to one in three Australian students now receives disability assistance in schools, with payments of up to $45,000 per student for those with the most severe needs.

    Public and private schools are receiving millions of dollars annually to boost the learning of students with physical, mental and socio-emotional disabilities, with the federal bill topping $5bn a year, the latest figures show.

    

    But parents say more can be done to support their children with additional needs as kids continue to fall through the gaps of mainstream schooling and questions remain about whether the funds are being properly spent by schools.

    

    The latest statistics from the Nationally Consistent Collection of Data (NCCD) on children with a disability shows 30.3 per cent of students are deemed by teachers to need an adjustment in their learning in South Australia – well above the 25.7 per cent national average, which itself is twice the rate of disability in children overall (around 12 per cent).

    

    In Victoria, 27.2 per cent of students are receiving disability help in schools, compared to 25.9 per cent in NSW, 23.6 per cent in the ACT and Queensland, 23.5 per cent in Western Australia and 21.8 per cent in Tasmania.

    

    Students in the Northern Territory are the highest overall, with 32.9 per cent receiving disability adjustments, although its unique demographics makes it hard to compare with other states.

    

    SCROLL DOWN FOR A STATE-BY-STATE BREAKDOWN

    

    The extra funding is allocated for students categorised by teachers and other educational professionals as needing support for physical, cognitive, sensory or social/emotional support.

    

    The NCCD funds come in addition to the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

    

    Funding is allocated according to supplementary need ($6076 for primary and $5999 for secondary), substantial need ($21,122 for primary and $21,089 for secondary) and extensive need ($45,137 for primary and $45,086 for secondary).

    

    Schools often pool the funding even though it is received on the basis of individual need. While a diagnosis helps secure funding, it is not necessary. Teachers and other classroom professionals use their professional judgment to determine the level of support needed.

    

    The lowest level of support, known as Quality Differentiated Teaching Practice, is not funded.

    

    Parents advised to advocate for their child

    

    Children and Young People with Disability Australia CEO Skye Kakoschke-Moore said parents needed to know the funding "doesn't work like an individual funding package and being included in the data doesn't automatically mean a child will receive a specific level of resourcing".

    

    "However, parents and caregivers have a legal right under the Disability Standards for Education to be involved in decisions about their child's education and to understand what supports are in place at school. That includes being part of conversations with educators about reasonable adjustments, learning plans, and how their child is being supported day-to-day," she said.

    

    Australian Christian College Marsden Park learning support coordinator Anne-Louise Clark said it's crucial parents advocate for their child to ensure they get the level of support, adjustments and funding they require.

    

    "Regular and ongoing communication is vital," she said.

    

    "Always speak up before something becomes big – small concerns are easier to address than big problems. Schools want students to be the best possible version of themselves, just like parents do."

    

    Victorian disability advocate Julie Phillips advises parents to ask schools about the level of funding their children may be getting.

    

    "Many of my parents, when I asked them whether their kids are getting funding under the NCCD and how much, they don't actually know," she said.

    

    "A lot of the schools make these applications without even letting the parents know."

    

    'Not enough funding for kids like my son'

    

    Adelaide year 5 student Jerzy Ashley has attended St Michael's College at Beverly since reception.

    

    He has cerebral palsy and complex health needs and receives both NDIS and NCCD funding.

    

    Mum Emma Ashley said that meant her son could receive extra support to adjust lessons, attend camps and perform in the school musical.

    

    "He has initially faced barriers and challenges ... but he has had incredible support as well," she said.

    

    "He's had certain teachers and education support officers that have gone above and beyond to make sure that he is included. And it means that he's meaningfully taking part in school life."

    

    Sydney mum Karlha Borg, 30, says better funding could have kept her seven-year-old son Bowie Goul in mainstream schooling.

    

    Bowie has ADHD, a condition that meant he only ever completed two full days of school from kindergarten to year 1, according to Ms Borg.

    

    "He had a very bad experience of schooling," his mum said.

    

    "They couldn't handle his behaviour, he would correct the teacher and pretended he could not read or write."

    

    Ms Borg said Bowie is highly intelligent and since being taken out of mainstream schooling and starting distance education at Australian Christian College, Marsden Park, he is "thriving".

    

    "There's not enough funding for kids like my son," she said.

    

    "If he had additional funding he would've had someone to provide one-on-one support to help him, someone who understands him.

    

    "He learns differently and needs that support. He could've succeeded in the mainstream."

    

    How much are private schools getting?

    

    The latest data, which is for 2024, shows total disability funding for all private schools rose from $674m in 2014 to $2.4bn in 2024 – an increase of 256 per cent.

    

    The federal government also gives disability funding to states for public schools.

    

    States received $187m in 2014, rising to $1.6bn in 2024, the latest government figures show.

    

    Apart from block grants given to school organisations such as the Catholic Education Commission, the mainstream private school with the highest disability funding is Tyndale Christian School in Adelaide's northern suburbs, which received $4.4m in disability funding in 2024.

    

    New South Wales

    

    The NSW mainstream private school with the highest individual disability funding is Belmont Christian College, which receives $2.8m, followed by Mater Dei School and Maitland Christian School, which also receives $2.8m, and Trinity Grammar ($2.6m).

    

    Other schools with substantial disability funding is Hunter Valley Grammar ($1.9m), Oxford Falls Grammar School ($1.9m) and Norwest Christian College ($1.8m).

    

    Specialist school St Lucy's School received $7.8m in funding.

    

    One of the highest in the ACT is Canberra Grammar, which received $2.1m and Canberra Girls' Grammar ($1.5m).

    

    The NSW government was also given $478m for public school disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Victoria

    

    The mainstream Victorian private school with the highest disability funding is leading co-ed provider Caulfield Grammar, which received $4m in 2024.

    

    Flinders Christian Community College Inc, which runs the autism-specialist Joshua Centre, received $5m.

    

    Special school Rossbourne School received $4.3m. Chairo Parent Governed Christian Education Limited ($3.5m), Community College Gippsland ($3.4m) and SEDA College ($2.9m) also received significant funding.

    

    Other major beneficiaries are Haileybury, which receives $2.9m, Woodleigh School ($2.9m), Donvale Christian College ($2.8m) and Melton Christian Centre ($2.6m).

    

    Other leading private schools receiving substantial funds include Ivanhoe Grammar, which receives $2.4m, Methodist Ladies' College ($2.1m), Girton Grammar ($2m) and Wesley College ($1.8m).

    

    A Caulfield Grammar spokesman said "annual funding variations reflect changes in student needs and government assessment processes".

    

    The Victorian government was also given $486m in 2024 for disability funding in public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Geelong schools receiving significant allocations include Geelong Christian Education Association (Covenant College), which received $2m in 2024, and Christian College Geelong ($1.9m).

    

    Queensland

    

    The highest level of disability funding in Queensland went to Men of Business Academy, which received $3.1m, followed by Emmanuel College ($2.8m) and Maryborough Christian Education Foundation ($2.5m), which has a day campus and distance education option.

    

    Other Queensland schools receiving substantial funds include Kings Christian College ($2m) and Cannon Hill Anglican College ($1.9m).

    

    Emmanuel College principal Dan Brown said two-thirds of the funding allocated to his school went to Josiah College, which is a specialist school supporting students on the autism spectrum.

    

    "This funding supports adjustments such as additional staff, learning support programs, allied health collaboration, and resources that enable students to access and engage with their learning," he said.

    

    The Queensland government was also given $350m in 2024 for public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    South Australia

    

    The school in SA with the highest individual funding allocation of $4.4m is Tyndale Christian School in Salisbury East, followed by Ngutu College, a specialist Indigenous college which receives $3.2m.

    

    Other leading schools with high federal disability funding include St Peter's College ($1.5m), St John's Grammar ($1.5m), Pembroke School ($1.4m) and Scotch College ($1.3m).

    

    The SA government received $111m in 2024 for public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Western Australia

    

    The WA school with the highest individual disability funding is John XXIII College which receives $2.7m, followed by Carey Baptist College ($2.6m) and Hale School ($1.7m).

    

    The WA government was also given $110m in 2024 for disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Northern Territory

    

    Individual schools receiving large funding grants for disability support in the NT include Haileybury Rendall ($1.6m), St Philip's College ($1.2) and Yipirinya School ($1.8m).

    

    In addition, NT Christian Schools were given $3.9m and Catholic schools $18m.

    

    The NT government was also given $34m in 2024 for disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

But one of the biggest problems, Deputy Speaker, always when you design these grand centralised systems, once you design them, they seemingly work well, at least in terms of the discussion in this parliament and in the documents designed by policymakers, but it's how they're utilised by people on the ground, legitimately or otherwise, that makes the material difference to whether Australians continue to have confidence, where they're respecting people where they they are, and they're seeking to empower people to live out their best lives. We've seen this in the context, obviously, in the IAEA. We've seen similar and parallel examples where people in Canberra think they can design programmes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders. And of course, we see them across many programmes in the disability sector where the organic development of services designed to support those often the most vulnerable in the community have slowly had their capacity corroded because the system has said you no longer fit within how we run programmatically. One of the great community services in the Goldstein electorate is Bailey House. is, I think, coming up 75th year this year or is in its 75th year this year. A great community organisation supporting people with a disability, in particular residents of nearby suburbs with Down syndrome. And I've always been a big supporter of Bailey House. It's an amazing community organisation full of people doing incredible work. But they're a support service that existed before the NDIS One of the biggest problems that they've had is that the NDIS has not been well designed to accommodate and meet the needs of centres like theirs because it doesn't reflect the design and the support and the cost structures that operate there. So they go out and fundraise, of course, as many disability and other community organisations do. But if there's an organisation that the NDIS should be working to empower, frankly, for efficiency, for scale, for service delivery, for better outcomes for people with a disability, for integrity measures, for just about every single thing they do fulfils an important gap around ownership, control of public money in a way and to be custodians for people with a disability to live out a better life. Bailey House fulfils that purpose just like their programme around Bailey Arts fulfils that that purpose and I'll never stop speaking highly of them because of the important role they play within the community and bring others in from the community to support people with a disability. That's what the NDIS should be seeking to empower, to support clients to be able to live out their best lives with the community services that they they need. But instead, it has been allowed to become a honeypot for fraudsters and the corrupt, to take advantage of the Australian taxpayer and, of course, people with a disability. The design failure right from the outset has caused huge losses of public money. I see one of the Labor members, who I assume is supporting this bill, smugly replying and dismissing such a comment. The government is literally introducing integrity and safeguard measures to address the design limitations and problems of the scheme. That has led led to, in the former Minister for Disability's own words, led to organised crime taking advantage of the Australian taxpayer and people with a disability. I don't think that's something that should be smugly dismissed. I think it should be acknowledged, fixed as quickly as possible. The only criticism I have is that this bill does not go far enough. It probably gives a sad reflection on why so many Labor members just shrug in indifference when we talk about $15 billion of money going to organised crime through the CFMEU Labor cartel. According to them, it says public money. And hey, we can just smugly dismiss the realities of what the Labor government seeks to empower. I think there's a time, Deputy Speaker, where we've got to acknowledge that the government has got something wrong. And when the government is turning around before the next federal federal budget and saying, Australians who have worked hard, saved and sacrificed to get themselves ahead for them and their families, that government wants to go around and then say, and we're going to add extra taxes on you, but we're not going to do anything about handing public money from the Treasury to organise crime through the CFMEU-Labour cartel. I actually think there's something really sick and kind of perverse about that. And the tidbit measures by comparison that the government is seeking to do with this bill on NDIS fraud and NDIS corruption, it doesn't surprise me, but it does disappoint me that the Labor Party, Labor members would smugly dismiss such a measure when we're talking about taking advantage of some of the most vulnerable people in the community, when those members need to reflect on the fact that it is public money that is being used for corrupt and fraudulent purposes, and more importantly, that within five weeks, we all know we're going to come into the parliament and they're going to propose that while they're indifferent to doing anything about public money going to organise crime, corruption and fraud, that that they'll have no hesitation in turning around and adding new taxes onto Australians to fund that organised crime, corruption and fraud. And so I think it is so important that we support these basic measures. But I do not think they're the end. And until this government starts to take organised crime, corruption and fraud from public programmes seriously—and they are not—how they could then turn around to the Australian taxpayer and even expect people to pay their current bills, let alone ask them to pay bigger bills for new taxes because they have no fiscal constraint, no preparedness to address fiscal programme design, and to raid the future opportunity and aspiration of Australians to feed the undeserving, being organised crime, corruption and fraud, I think is just frankly incredible. But welcome to the Albanese government, Deputy Speaker, because when it comes down to it and a choice between standing up for Australian taxpayers or handing money to organised crime, we know who they'll support.
I call the member for Bullwinkle. Thank you, Speaker. the NDIS is a national programme that funds care and support for people under 65 years of age with permanent and significant disabilities. And I rise today to speak on the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment, integrity and safeguarding, the Bill 2025. In my electorate of Bullwinkle, from the hills of Mundaring to the heart of the Western Wheatbelt towns and the Foothills communities, I see firsthand the transformative power of NDIS Australians are rightly proud of this scheme. It is a world-leading, life-changing pillar of our social fabric and for the families that I meet in my electorate the NDIS isn't just about policy. It's the difference between isolation and community, between a life of limitation and a life of independence. The NDIS is a life-changing scheme and today it helps more than 750,000 Australians live better and more dignified lives. It was Labor who created the NDIS and let there be no doubt that under Labor it is here to stay. As a registered nurse and midwife myself, I've spent my career caring for people when they are at their most vulnerable. I know that healthcare and disability support are built on a foundation foundation of trust because we value this scheme so deeply and we all have a collective responsibility to protect it. We must ensure that that it is sustainable, effective and safe. And most importantly, we must ensure that it operates with absolute integrity and that every cent goes towards the care that our community deserves. The system set up by the previous, continued by the previous government, lacked basic prevention controls for fraud and non-compliance.

Headline: Services' Easter safety advice
Full Text:
Colac and district emergency services are reminding the community to drive safe this Easter, with an expectation of increased traffic across the region.

    Operation Nexus will get underway tomorrow for the Easter long weekend, which will see police highly visible across the state's roads.

    The operation will see every available resource, from general duties through to highway patrol and specialist road policing units, deployed over the five-day statewide blitz.

    Colac Highway Patrol Sergeant Jake Andrews said officers would be targeting speed, impaired driving and behaviour offences.

    It follows multiple speed and behavioural offences across the Colac Otway region during the Labour Day long weekend last month.

    There will be a focus on major arterials heading to holiday hotspots, with lives lost on Victorian regional roads accounting for more than half of this year's fatalities.

    "It will be interesting to see if fuel makes a difference on how many people we see," Sgt Andrews said.

    "I think we are still expecting regardless that the coastal areas will be pretty busy, given it's the last opportunity before the weather gets too bad to get out."

    Sgt Andrews said Easter was always an issue because there were so many more people on the roads driving to campsites and holiday destinations.

    "Drive safe, look after one and another, and get to and from your destination without incident please," he said.

    Victoria Police said the chance of motorists being detected breaking the road rules had "drastically increased" following a recent uplift in road policing enforcement set to continue this weekend.

    There was a 30 per cent yearon-year increase in the number of infringements issued over last month's statewide road policing blitz over the Labour Day long weekend, with police detecting 6442 offences across four days.

    Police also recorded a 26-percent increase in patrol hours for the operation, compared to the same period the previous year.

    Meanwhile, Lorne SES Unit's Chris Jones reminded coastal motorists to be realistic with their journey deadlines.

    "If you're tired, stop immediately don't push through," he said.

    "This could be the difference between life and death. Stay extra alert, drive according to the conditions, take more frequent breaks and stay safe.

    "We want you to arrive safely and not meet you by accident."

    VICSES urges drivers to plan breaks every two hours and swap drivers where possible.

    It comes as Lorne SES marks almost one year since responding to a major motorcycle crash on the Great Ocean Road.

    Mr Jones and fellow member Phil Walsh found the driver injured and trapped in a gully, prompting an extensive multi-agency emergency response to retrieve him.

    The driver reunited with Mr Jones this week to thank the volunteers who responded to assist him.

    Colac's Driver Reviver site on Murray Street will be open across the Easter long weekend from the afternoon through to the evening, starting tomorrow.

Headline: Street program works begin
Full Text:
PEDESTRIANS and motorists will soon benefit from two road safety improvement projects in Kerang.

    Work started last week on the projects thanks to the Victorian Government though the Safe Local Roads and Streets Program, which is providing $210 million across Victoria to improve the safety of local roads.

    As part of the program, speed reduction measures will be placed along Wyndham Street, Kerang, either side of Victoria Street.

    The school crossing at Boundary Street, Kerang, near Mitchell Street, will also be replaced with a raised priority crossing to improve pedestrian safety and increase visibility.

    As part of the school crossing improvements, the crossing will be closed to all traffic from 24 March to 2 April, as well as between 7 April and 9 April.

    Motorists are advised to use Bendigo Road or the Murray Valley Highway if travelling between Airport Road and Wellington Street, or Croton Street, Dunlop Street, Lyall Avenue, Marne Street or Mitchell Street if accessing local roads.

    Meanwhile, reduced speed limits and traffic management controls will be in place at the intersection of Victoria and Wyndham streets until Friday, 17 April as part of the improvements.

    The Safe Local Roads and Streets Program will also support the following projects, with details regarding start dates and changed traffic conditions to be announced closer to when these works begin:

    - Improvements to the intersection of Cohuna Island and Tennis roads, Cohuna, including the installation of raised pedestrian crossings either side of Apex Park.

    - The installation of a roundabout and speed reduction measures at the intersection of Channel and Market streets, Cohuna.

    - The placement of a roundabout, raised pedestrian crossings and speed reduction measures at the intersection of Maxwell, Shadforth and Wyndham streets, Kerang.

Fresh concerns over the safety of the Kiewa Valley Highway and need for "urgent action" have been raised in the Victorian parliament.

    "The road is an absolute disgrace, and the Victorian government should hang its head in shame for allowing such an appalling failure of basic road maintenance.

    "Our regional roads should be safe for everyone and the current condition of the Kiewa Valley Highway is simply not good enough."

    Mr McCurdy said the community deserves better and called for urgent action to improve road safety.

    "Regional Victorians aren't asking for special treatment; we're asking for safe, well-maintained roads," he said.

Headline: A Key Step To Implement Moriac Structure Plan
Full Text:
Surf Coast Shire Council will request an independent panel to consider submissions on a planning scheme amendment that will guide land use and development decisions in Moriac over the next decade.

    Council made the decision at its 24 March Council meeting, which welcomed 36 community members to Modewarre Memorial Hall.

    The proposed amendment known as Amendment C145surf Moriac Structure Plan 2023 Implementation will introduce a new framework plan and local policies into the Surf Coast Planning Scheme.

    It was placed on public exhibition from 18 September to 19 October 2025, with six submissions made.

    Two relating to the direction of future growth within the town were unresolved, prompting Council to refer the submissions to an independent panel to ensure the views are properly considered.

    Surf Coast Shire Councillor Adrian Schonfelder thanked all submitters.

    "The highly engaged Moriac community was vital in shaping the Moriac Structure Plan, telling us that residential development should be incremental to help protect the town's treasured rural character," Cr Schonfelder said.

    "This amendment will enable us to implement the key strategies and actions from the structure plan into our planning scheme, so we want to make sure each view is carefully considered before it's adopted."

    Council will request the Minister for Planning to appoint an independent panel.

    "We look forward to receiving the panel's report and the recommendations," Cr Schonfelder said.

    Council was supportive of a change requested in a Department of Transport and Planning submission. It responds to community road safety concerns and seeks to limit the number of new lots with direct access from Hendy Main Road. Instead, access would be via new internal roads.

    Corangamite Catchment Management Authority lodged a supporting submission.

Headline: State lagging on e-bike rules
Full Text:
Victoria is falling behind other states on e-bike safety, as New South Wales and Queensland roll out tough new crackdowns while local councils grapple with rising concerns.

    Last week, the New South Wales Government announced plans to give police sweeping powers to seize and destroy illegal, overpow ered, and unregistered e-bikes caught speeding, fuelling dangerous anti-social behaviour and serious injuries.

    Meanwhile, Queensland will ban children under 16 from riding e-bikes and e-scooters and require riders to hold at least a learner permit.

    By contrast, Victoria has no minimum age requirement for e-bike riders and does not require registration or licensing.

    The gap is being felt locally at Wilson Botanic Park, where the City of Casey has reported an increase in the use of e-bikes and motorbikes within Wilson Botanic Park in recent months.

    "These vehicles pose a serious safety risk to park users," council told residents in a letter on 5 March.

    "To help prevent the entry of e-bikes and other prohibited vehicles, staff presence at park gates was initially increased during peak periods.

    "While this approach was effective when staff were onsite, e-bikes and motorbikes have continued to enter the park after hours.

    "Over the past two weeks, this has resulted in significant damage to park grounds and plantings, as well as numerous reports from visitors raising concerns about safety," The problem has been ongoing since mid2025 when staff first observed illegal bikes entering Wilson Botanic Park through the Princes Highway and Bournevale Drive entrances.

    It escalated last December when councillors approved the overflow carpark, overriding officer recommendations and the majority of community feedback.

    Council is working closely with key stakeholders to address this issue, including looking at practical ways to prevent unauthorised vehicle access at Wilson Botanic Park Berwick.

    "The safety of our community is our top priority, and Council supports current Victorian legislation and Victoria Police initiatives aimed at improving safety on our roads and shared paths," Casey Mayor Cr Stefan Koomen added.

    "We acknowledge recent initiatives in New South Wales and Queensland and believe these are timely and worth assessing for potential application in Victoria."

and to support homebuyers in Victoria. On this side, we are so proud of all of that work. We're very proud of the world-leading work we have done to remove combustible cladding here in in Victoria.
