The member may have the call when the matter is next before the chair. The question is that the house now adjourns. And I call on members to raise adjournment matters.
Member for Eildon. I have a matter for priority to improve line markings on the Whittlesea King Lake Road right across the King Lake Ranges before winter sets in. The line markings now are almost invisible. The cat's eyes in many places are worn out or damaged, further reducing visibility and safety. Luminescent markings have faded and lost any effectiveness. The King Lake Ranges is known for its unique weather. Heavy fog is a feature and so safe roads are paramount during the day and at night. These much needed improvements are simple and should be a no-brainer. Many raise the condition of this road with me. Potholes are a constant and the dangerous... Now, equally, the line markings are dangerous. A long-time emergency services volunteer who travels this road frequently contacted me recently about her concern. She knows this road, drives it regularly and understands the risks and hazards and her message is stark. With fog now rolling into King Lake, she says, the current state of line markings is a recipe for disaster. Driving the Whittlesea King Lake Road in heavy fog, which was 7.30am two weeks ago, she described needing intense concentration simply to keep her car on the road. The lines, she says, are almost invisible. And she says it's the worst that she has encountered. And this is not an abstract concern. This is someone responding to emergencies, often at night, in poor conditions, on a narrow, winding and somewhat unforgiving road. In those conditions, line markings are not cosmetic. They are critical. When visibility drops, they are often the only guide a driver has. The government has trialled new technologies on a number of segments of this road, including enhanced and luminescent markings. In the end, that trial, like the visibility on this stretch, simply faded away. But what matters to drivers on the ground is simple. Can they see the the road? And right now, they can't. And the community knows it. The consistent message is that this road needs to be more than patchwork fixes and routine maintenance. It needs clear, visible, well-maintained line markings that perform in real conditions, at night, in fog, and on a road where mistakes are unforgiving. eyes are crucial for delineating lanes at night and in poor weather and their deterioration can cause significant visibility issues for motorists. Missing or damaged road studs can make it difficult to see the road ahead in low light or wet weather. Before winter sets in and fog becomes a daily hazard, the Minister must act. Because when a frontline volunteer is telling you the road is unsafe, you don't want to wait for a report. You fix it. And the question is simple. Will the government act now or wait until somebody is seriously injured or worse before it does?
Thank you very much Speaker and my adjournment matter this evening is for the Minister for Skills Skills and TAFE in the other place and the action I seek is for the Minister to update the House on how the government is acting to enhance Victorian university governance. Now, I recently received some correspondence from a constituent named Thomas. And Thomas is studying law at Monash University just down the road and recently commenced his second year. Thomas, like many of his peers, was shocked to be told last October by the university that tutorials would be discontinued for all but first year students. Now, I understand this decision was made without any prior consultation with students or the Monash Law Student Society. Thomas has conveyed to us his fears about the impact this will have on his future as a lawyer. The students are missing out on essential collaborative work, discussions of learnings and practical and analytical skills that are fundamental to the legal profession. I thank Thomas for reaching out with his cohorts. Now, one may also wonder, apparently I've heard that Monash did not stop the tutorials for the medical students. So one may wonder, do they think, and obviously our doctors are very important, they're trained just like our lawyers and other people. So you wonder whether Monash are wondering or thinking to themselves that, oh, we better not do it for medicine because that might have other effects. But I would put to Monash to consider that stopping tutorials for legal students, have they thought of any other effects that might have? Our lawyers are accredited, they need to do proper work and as much as sometimes they have a bad rap, we need our lawyers to be skilled and excellent. So I believe a committee of the house is currently conducting an inquiry into enhancing Victorian university governance, including through elevating student voice at the higher level. And a shout-out to the NTUU, who are doing some good work in this area as well. Removing tutorials without consultation is the kind of action I would hope would not happen when student voice is elevated at universities. I look forward to the minister's response.
The member for Euroa Thank you, Speaker. My adjournment this evening is for the minister for roads. And the action I seek is for it to come for a drive with Broadford local legend Archie Baines in one of his trucks and see firsthand the state of our local roads. It might sound like a nice invitation speaker but it is anything but. It is pretty dangerous. The shocking and deteriorating condition of our roads is incredibly serious. So I want to tell you about Archie. Baines is 82-year-old, a highly experienced truck driver with decades behind him, the kind of man that knows our roads better than most. On Sunday 22 March, after attending the Kyabra McMaster, Archie was driving along the Ngambi Bypass at the Goulburn Valley Highway, a major arterial road, a key freight route, a road that should be safe. And as he approached the first Ngambi Overpass, his truck struck a large pothole in the right-hand wheel track, and within moments his steer tyre blew out. And what followed could have been fatal. His truck was dragged across the lanes, taking out about 100 metres of fencing and safety barriers. And there was significant damage to his truck and the vehicle he was towing, but by sheer luck, Archie survived. Another local driver, just behind him in a new vehicle hit the exact same pothole. Multiple tyre blowouts, two incidences, the same stretch of road, the same hazard. What's concerning for every Victorian is the pothole had already been marked, ringed in white paint, painted but not repaired. And this is exactly why people are seeing across the state. Circles of paint everywhere like warnings but nothing is ever fixed. How many more circles of paint do we need before something is actually repaired? How many more warnings do the Allen Labor Government need before it acts? Next time we may not be talking about a damaged truck, we may be talking about a life lost. Archie's story is one of many. Shay, travelling the Violet Town to Murchison Road four times a week for essential therapy, is navigating a road that is putting her at risk every trip. Corey hit a pothole in Anzac Avenue in Seymour. He hit it so hard he bent his rim and now has the most expensive hose reel that you can purchase. Julie, between Heathcote and Ngambi, has taken upon herself to mark the potholes with her own paint. And across from Benalla to Yarrawonga and Avenal to Ngambi, the roads are unsafe. Pothole after pothole, rough patch after rough patch. When someone like Archie, with decades of experience, is nearly taken out by a pothole on a major highway, that should be the wake-up call. He was incredibly lucky, and seconds later it could have been fatal. He could have gone on to a railway embankment and the outcome catastrophic. Our communities communities deserve safe roads. Our freight operators deserve infrastructure that reflects the critical role they play and our families deserve to know that they will make it home safely. Minister, come for a drive, see it first hand, get into a truck with Archie and let him show you the state of our roads properly. Thank you Speaker.
My adjournment matter is for the Minister for Consumer Affairs and the action I seek is for the Minister to provide an update on how the Fairfield Taskforce will operate in growth areas like Melton and to consider Melton as the first or early location for Taskforce activity so local residents can see these new protections in action. This issue is front of mind for many families in Melton. Fuel prices and the pressure they place on household budgets. In a growing community like Melton, people rely on their cars every day. Getting to work, school or appointments is not optional, it's essential. When fuel prices spike, families feel it immediately. I welcome the Alan Labor government's anti-price gouging laws and ServoSaver. These reforms give motorists transparency and the ability to plan ahead. I have long called for action on fuel pricing in Melton and requiring retailers to set a 24-hour maximum price as a practical step that gives drivers certainty.

Full Text: Ms Lover? My question is for the Minister for Transport Infrastructure. When will the Minister improve safety for pedestrians walking to the bus stop at the intersection of Yanyin Road and Doctors Gully Road? I have been contacted by several parents of children who catch a school bus on Yanyin Road near the roundabout at the intersection with Doctors Gully Road. Parents drop their kids along Doctors Gully Road who then walk around the corner to the bus stop. But access is now restricted on Doctors Gully Road due to the construction of the Yanyin Road upgrade and a recent car crash damaged the footpath, which has been closed off. This forces children to walk all the way around the roundabout, crossing several lanes with heavy traffic, where there are no refuge islands and no crossing supervisors. DTP wrote to a parent to say that the project operator suggested a zebra crossing would be a suitable safety enhancement and this should be raised with the relevant authority. The minister must take urgent action to improve safety at this intersection which has become dangerous for pedestrians.

News
Urgent actions needed on drugs in regional communities in Victoria. That's the call from Northern Victoria MP Gail Broad. She says the personal stories she's heard from use and harm from drugs are devastating. Widespread drug use is contributing to rising crime, to road trauma and family violence, as well as increasing pressure on our hospitals and ambulance services. Now in many small regional towns, mental health services simply don't exist. And the Nats say they'll oppose any plan to expand the Federal Parliament, warning it may cost taxpayers more than $620 million. Mally mp Anne Webster says Aussies are already under financial pressure and need practical solutions, not more pollies. Triple m National News. Hey, I'm Michaela Savage.

Headline: Australian schools are getting $5bn a year in disability funding – search the list and get expert tips on accessing support for your child
Full Text:
Nearly one in three students are now classed as disabled, reaping billions of dollars in extra funding for schools. See how much top private schools get and how your child can access more support. 

    WATCH NOW: Education Unpacked part two - Educating diverse minds

    

    A must-watch two-part conversation hosted by Dr Susie O'Brien.

    

    Up to one in three Australian students now receives disability assistance in schools, with payments of up to $45,000 per student for those with the most severe needs.

    

    Public and private schools are receiving millions of dollars annually to boost the learning of students with physical, mental and socio-emotional disabilities, with the federal bill topping $5bn a year, the latest figures show.

    

    But parents say more can be done to support their children with additional needs as kids continue to fall through the gaps of mainstream schooling and questions remain about whether the funds are being properly spent by schools.

    

    The latest statistics from the Nationally Consistent Collection of Data (NCCD) on children with a disability shows 30.3 per cent of students are deemed by teachers to need an adjustment in their learning in South Australia – well above the 25.7 per cent national average, which itself is twice the rate of disability in children overall (around 12 per cent).

    

    In Victoria, 27.2 per cent of students are receiving disability help in schools, compared to 25.9 per cent in NSW, 23.6 per cent in the ACT and Queensland, 23.5 per cent in Western Australia and 21.8 per cent in Tasmania.

    

    Students in the Northern Territory are the highest overall, with 32.9 per cent receiving disability adjustments, although its unique demographics makes it hard to compare with other states.

    

    SCROLL DOWN FOR A STATE-BY-STATE BREAKDOWN

    

    The extra funding is allocated for students categorised by teachers and other educational professionals as needing support for physical, cognitive, sensory or social/emotional support.

    

    The NCCD funds come in addition to the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

    

    Funding is allocated according to supplementary need ($6076 for primary and $5999 for secondary), substantial need ($21,122 for primary and $21,089 for secondary) and extensive need ($45,137 for primary and $45,086 for secondary).

    

    Schools often pool the funding even though it is received on the basis of individual need. While a diagnosis helps secure funding, it is not necessary. Teachers and other classroom professionals use their professional judgment to determine the level of support needed.

    

    The lowest level of support, known as Quality Differentiated Teaching Practice, is not funded.

    

    Parents advised to advocate for their child

    

    Children and Young People with Disability Australia CEO Skye Kakoschke-Moore said parents needed to know the funding "doesn't work like an individual funding package and being included in the data doesn't automatically mean a child will receive a specific level of resourcing".

    

    "However, parents and caregivers have a legal right under the Disability Standards for Education to be involved in decisions about their child's education and to understand what supports are in place at school. That includes being part of conversations with educators about reasonable adjustments, learning plans, and how their child is being supported day-to-day," she said.

    

    Australian Christian College Marsden Park learning support coordinator Anne-Louise Clark said it's crucial parents advocate for their child to ensure they get the level of support, adjustments and funding they require.

    

    "Regular and ongoing communication is vital," she said.

    

    "Always speak up before something becomes big – small concerns are easier to address than big problems. Schools want students to be the best possible version of themselves, just like parents do."

    

    Victorian disability advocate Julie Phillips advises parents to ask schools about the level of funding their children may be getting.

    

    "Many of my parents, when I asked them whether their kids are getting funding under the NCCD and how much, they don't actually know," she said.

    

    "A lot of the schools make these applications without even letting the parents know."

    

    'Not enough funding for kids like my son'

    

    Adelaide year 5 student Jerzy Ashley has attended St Michael's College at Beverly since reception.

    

    He has cerebral palsy and complex health needs and receives both NDIS and NCCD funding.

    

    Mum Emma Ashley said that meant her son could receive extra support to adjust lessons, attend camps and perform in the school musical.

    

    "He has initially faced barriers and challenges ... but he has had incredible support as well," she said.

    

    "He's had certain teachers and education support officers that have gone above and beyond to make sure that he is included. And it means that he's meaningfully taking part in school life."

    

    Sydney mum Karlha Borg, 30, says better funding could have kept her seven-year-old son Bowie Goul in mainstream schooling.

    

    Bowie has ADHD, a condition that meant he only ever completed two full days of school from kindergarten to year 1, according to Ms Borg.

    

    "He had a very bad experience of schooling," his mum said.

    

    "They couldn't handle his behaviour, he would correct the teacher and pretended he could not read or write."

    

    Ms Borg said Bowie is highly intelligent and since being taken out of mainstream schooling and starting distance education at Australian Christian College, Marsden Park, he is "thriving".

    

    "There's not enough funding for kids like my son," she said.

    

    "If he had additional funding he would've had someone to provide one-on-one support to help him, someone who understands him.

    

    "He learns differently and needs that support. He could've succeeded in the mainstream."

    

    How much are private schools getting?

    

    The latest data, which is for 2024, shows total disability funding for all private schools rose from $674m in 2014 to $2.4bn in 2024 – an increase of 256 per cent.

    

    The federal government also gives disability funding to states for public schools.

    

    States received $187m in 2014, rising to $1.6bn in 2024, the latest government figures show.

    

    Apart from block grants given to school organisations such as the Catholic Education Commission, the mainstream private school with the highest disability funding is Tyndale Christian School in Adelaide's northern suburbs, which received $4.4m in disability funding in 2024.

    

    New South Wales

    

    The NSW mainstream private school with the highest individual disability funding is Belmont Christian College, which receives $2.8m, followed by Mater Dei School and Maitland Christian School, which also receives $2.8m, and Trinity Grammar ($2.6m).

    

    Other schools with substantial disability funding is Hunter Valley Grammar ($1.9m), Oxford Falls Grammar School ($1.9m) and Norwest Christian College ($1.8m).

    

    Specialist school St Lucy's School received $7.8m in funding.

    

    One of the highest in the ACT is Canberra Grammar, which received $2.1m and Canberra Girls' Grammar ($1.5m).

    

    The NSW government was also given $478m for public school disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Victoria

    

    The mainstream Victorian private school with the highest disability funding is leading co-ed provider Caulfield Grammar, which received $4m in 2024.

    

    Flinders Christian Community College Inc, which runs the autism-specialist Joshua Centre, received $5m.

    

    Special school Rossbourne School received $4.3m. Chairo Parent Governed Christian Education Limited ($3.5m), Community College Gippsland ($3.4m) and SEDA College ($2.9m) also received significant funding.

    

    Other major beneficiaries are Haileybury, which receives $2.9m, Woodleigh School ($2.9m), Donvale Christian College ($2.8m) and Melton Christian Centre ($2.6m).

    

    Other leading private schools receiving substantial funds include Ivanhoe Grammar, which receives $2.4m, Methodist Ladies' College ($2.1m), Girton Grammar ($2m) and Wesley College ($1.8m).

    

    A Caulfield Grammar spokesman said "annual funding variations reflect changes in student needs and government assessment processes".

    

    The Victorian government was also given $486m in 2024 for disability funding in public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Geelong schools receiving significant allocations include Geelong Christian Education Association (Covenant College), which received $2m in 2024, and Christian College Geelong ($1.9m).

    

    Queensland

    

    The highest level of disability funding in Queensland went to Men of Business Academy, which received $3.1m, followed by Emmanuel College ($2.8m) and Maryborough Christian Education Foundation ($2.5m), which has a day campus and distance education option.

    

    Other Queensland schools receiving substantial funds include Kings Christian College ($2m) and Cannon Hill Anglican College ($1.9m).

    

    Emmanuel College principal Dan Brown said two-thirds of the funding allocated to his school went to Josiah College, which is a specialist school supporting students on the autism spectrum.

    

    "This funding supports adjustments such as additional staff, learning support programs, allied health collaboration, and resources that enable students to access and engage with their learning," he said.

    

    The Queensland government was also given $350m in 2024 for public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    South Australia

    

    The school in SA with the highest individual funding allocation of $4.4m is Tyndale Christian School in Salisbury East, followed by Ngutu College, a specialist Indigenous college which receives $3.2m.

    

    Other leading schools with high federal disability funding include St Peter's College ($1.5m), St John's Grammar ($1.5m), Pembroke School ($1.4m) and Scotch College ($1.3m).

    

    The SA government received $111m in 2024 for public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Western Australia

    

    The WA school with the highest individual disability funding is John XXIII College which receives $2.7m, followed by Carey Baptist College ($2.6m) and Hale School ($1.7m).

    

    The WA government was also given $110m in 2024 for disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Northern Territory

    

    Individual schools receiving large funding grants for disability support in the NT include Haileybury Rendall ($1.6m), St Philip's College ($1.2) and Yipirinya School ($1.8m).

    

    In addition, NT Christian Schools were given $3.9m and Catholic schools $18m.

    

    The NT government was also given $34m in 2024 for disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Is your child getting enough disability support in schools? Email us at education@news.com.au

Headline: Australian schools are getting $5bn a year in disability funding – search the list and get expert tips on accessing support for your child
Full Text:
Nearly one in three students are now classed as disabled, reaping billions of dollars in extra funding for schools. See how much top private schools get and how your child can access more support. 

    Up to one in three Australian students now receives disability assistance in schools, with payments of up to $45,000 per student for those with the most severe needs.

    

    Public and private schools are receiving millions of dollars annually to boost the learning of students with physical, mental and socio-emotional disabilities, with the federal bill topping $5bn a year, the latest figures show.

    

    But parents say more can be done to support their children with additional needs as kids continue to fall through the gaps of mainstream schooling and questions remain about whether the funds are being properly spent by schools.

    

    The latest statistics from the Nationally Consistent Collection of Data (NCCD) on children with a disability shows 30.3 per cent of students are deemed by teachers to need an adjustment in their learning in South Australia – well above the 25.7 per cent national average, which itself is twice the rate of disability in children overall (around 12 per cent).

    

    In Victoria, 27.2 per cent of students are receiving disability help in schools, compared to 25.9 per cent in NSW, 23.6 per cent in the ACT and Queensland, 23.5 per cent in Western Australia and 21.8 per cent in Tasmania.

    

    Students in the Northern Territory are the highest overall, with 32.9 per cent receiving disability adjustments, although its unique demographics makes it hard to compare with other states.

    

    SCROLL DOWN FOR A STATE-BY-STATE BREAKDOWN

    

    The extra funding is allocated for students categorised by teachers and other educational professionals as needing support for physical, cognitive, sensory or social/emotional support.

    

    The NCCD funds come in addition to the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

    

    Funding is allocated according to supplementary need ($6076 for primary and $5999 for secondary), substantial need ($21,122 for primary and $21,089 for secondary) and extensive need ($45,137 for primary and $45,086 for secondary).

    

    Schools often pool the funding even though it is received on the basis of individual need. While a diagnosis helps secure funding, it is not necessary. Teachers and other classroom professionals use their professional judgment to determine the level of support needed.

    

    The lowest level of support, known as Quality Differentiated Teaching Practice, is not funded.

    

    Parents advised to advocate for their child

    

    Children and Young People with Disability Australia CEO Skye Kakoschke-Moore said parents needed to know the funding "doesn't work like an individual funding package and being included in the data doesn't automatically mean a child will receive a specific level of resourcing".

    

    "However, parents and caregivers have a legal right under the Disability Standards for Education to be involved in decisions about their child's education and to understand what supports are in place at school. That includes being part of conversations with educators about reasonable adjustments, learning plans, and how their child is being supported day-to-day," she said.

    

    Australian Christian College Marsden Park learning support coordinator Anne-Louise Clark said it's crucial parents advocate for their child to ensure they get the level of support, adjustments and funding they require.

    

    "Regular and ongoing communication is vital," she said.

    

    "Always speak up before something becomes big – small concerns are easier to address than big problems. Schools want students to be the best possible version of themselves, just like parents do."

    

    Victorian disability advocate Julie Phillips advises parents to ask schools about the level of funding their children may be getting.

    

    "Many of my parents, when I asked them whether their kids are getting funding under the NCCD and how much, they don't actually know," she said.

    

    "A lot of the schools make these applications without even letting the parents know."

    

    'Not enough funding for kids like my son'

    

    Adelaide year 5 student Jerzy Ashley has attended St Michael's College at Beverly since reception.

    

    He has cerebral palsy and complex health needs and receives both NDIS and NCCD funding.

    

    Mum Emma Ashley said that meant her son could receive extra support to adjust lessons, attend camps and perform in the school musical.

    

    "He has initially faced barriers and challenges ... but he has had incredible support as well," she said.

    

    "He's had certain teachers and education support officers that have gone above and beyond to make sure that he is included. And it means that he's meaningfully taking part in school life."

    

    Sydney mum Karlha Borg, 30, says better funding could have kept her seven-year-old son Bowie Goul in mainstream schooling.

    

    Bowie has ADHD, a condition that meant he only ever completed two full days of school from kindergarten to year 1, according to Ms Borg.

    

    "He had a very bad experience of schooling," his mum said.

    

    "They couldn't handle his behaviour, he would correct the teacher and pretended he could not read or write."

    

    Ms Borg said Bowie is highly intelligent and since being taken out of mainstream schooling and starting distance education at Australian Christian College, Marsden Park, he is "thriving".

    

    "There's not enough funding for kids like my son," she said.

    

    "If he had additional funding he would've had someone to provide one-on-one support to help him, someone who understands him.

    

    "He learns differently and needs that support. He could've succeeded in the mainstream."

    

    How much are private schools getting?

    

    The latest data, which is for 2024, shows total disability funding for all private schools rose from $674m in 2014 to $2.4bn in 2024 – an increase of 256 per cent.

    

    The federal government also gives disability funding to states for public schools.

    

    States received $187m in 2014, rising to $1.6bn in 2024, the latest government figures show.

    

    Apart from block grants given to school organisations such as the Catholic Education Commission, the mainstream private school with the highest disability funding is Tyndale Christian School in Adelaide's northern suburbs, which received $4.4m in disability funding in 2024.

    

    New South Wales

    

    The NSW mainstream private school with the highest individual disability funding is Belmont Christian College, which receives $2.8m, followed by Mater Dei School and Maitland Christian School, which also receives $2.8m, and Trinity Grammar ($2.6m).

    

    Other schools with substantial disability funding is Hunter Valley Grammar ($1.9m), Oxford Falls Grammar School ($1.9m) and Norwest Christian College ($1.8m).

    

    Specialist school St Lucy's School received $7.8m in funding.

    

    One of the highest in the ACT is Canberra Grammar, which received $2.1m and Canberra Girls' Grammar ($1.5m).

    

    The NSW government was also given $478m for public school disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

    Victoria

    

    The mainstream Victorian private school with the highest disability funding is leading co-ed provider Caulfield Grammar, which received $4m in 2024.

    

    Flinders Christian Community College Inc, which runs the autism-specialist Joshua Centre, received $5m.

    

    Special school Rossbourne School received $4.3m. Chairo Parent Governed Christian Education Limited ($3.5m), Community College Gippsland ($3.4m) and SEDA College ($2.9m) also received significant funding.

    

    Other major beneficiaries are Haileybury, which receives $2.9m, Woodleigh School ($2.9m), Donvale Christian College ($2.8m) and Melton Christian Centre ($2.6m).

    

    Other leading private schools receiving substantial funds include Ivanhoe Grammar, which receives $2.4m, Methodist Ladies' College ($2.1m), Girton Grammar ($2m) and Wesley College ($1.8m).

    

    A Caulfield Grammar spokesman said "annual funding variations reflect changes in student needs and government assessment processes".

    

    The Victorian government was also given $486m in 2024 for disability funding in public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Geelong schools receiving significant allocations include Geelong Christian Education Association (Covenant College), which received $2m in 2024, and Christian College Geelong ($1.9m).

    

    Queensland

    

    The highest level of disability funding in Queensland went to Men of Business Academy, which received $3.1m, followed by Emmanuel College ($2.8m) and Maryborough Christian Education Foundation ($2.5m), which has a day campus and distance education option.

    

    Other Queensland schools receiving substantial funds include Kings Christian College ($2m) and Cannon Hill Anglican College ($1.9m).

    

    Emmanuel College principal Dan Brown said two-thirds of the funding allocated to his school went to Josiah College, which is a specialist school supporting students on the autism spectrum.

    

    "This funding supports adjustments such as additional staff, learning support programs, allied health collaboration, and resources that enable students to access and engage with their learning," he said.

    

    The Queensland government was also given $350m in 2024 for public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    South Australia

    

    The school in SA with the highest individual funding allocation of $4.4m is Tyndale Christian School in Salisbury East, followed by Ngutu College, a specialist Indigenous college which receives $3.2m.

    

    Other leading schools with high federal disability funding include St Peter's College ($1.5m), St John's Grammar ($1.5m), Pembroke School ($1.4m) and Scotch College ($1.3m).

    

    The SA government received $111m in 2024 for public schools, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Western Australia

    

    The WA school with the highest individual disability funding is John XXIII College which receives $2.7m, followed by Carey Baptist College ($2.6m) and Hale School ($1.7m).

    

    The WA government was also given $110m in 2024 for disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

    

    Northern Territory

    

    Individual schools receiving large funding grants for disability support in the NT include Haileybury Rendall ($1.6m), St Philip's College ($1.2) and Yipirinya School ($1.8m).

    

    In addition, NT Christian Schools were given $3.9m and Catholic schools $18m.

    

    The NT government was also given $34m in 2024 for disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

Full Text:

   and claims of missing money, with Home Affairs refusing to say what it did the first time it was made aware of the situation, and ASIC declining to act on the second warning.

    

    Home Affairs received an anonymous tip-off in March 2021 alleging financial misconduct by Lenard Swanepoel-Trollip and later referred the information to the Administrative Review Tribunal, an independent federal body that reviews government decisions.

    

    That referral was made during the application process for permanent Australian visas initiated by Lenard, 44, in May 2019 on behalf of himself and his husband Christiaan Swanepoel-Trollip, 58.

    

    The tribunal's published decision in September 2023 stated the "anonymous on-line tip off" alleged Lenard had been involved in the "wrongful appropriation of funds" in South Africa connected to a real estate business, before the pair settled in Australia in 2017.

    

    Lenard was invited to respond, but did not contest the allegation during the proceedings. As the information did not form part of the reasons for the decision, the tribunal did not place any weight upon it.

    

    Tribunal member Penelope Hunter affirmed a previous decision to reject the visas and did not make findings on the misconduct allegation, the decision states.

    

    Lenard, on behalf of the couple, has rejected any allegation of wrongdoing, fund misappropriation, phoenixing allegations or improper conduct.

    

    "The decision you reference contains no adverse finding against me whatsoever," he told this masthead.

    

    "The anonymous allegation referred to in that decision was expressly disregarded by the Tribunal, placed no weight upon, and formed no part of the reasons for the outcome."

    

    The allegation echoes findings from a liquidator's report into the collapse of the pair's South African business, Beyers Realty Group, in 2016, which identified the alleged movement of client trust money into other bank accounts.

    

    Lenard had said it was an innocent mistake, stating in an affidavit: "I accept I made a mistake in my conduct utilising the trust account funds to support the growth of the business."

    

    Further, internal emails seen by this masthead, separate to the tribunal proceedings, show corporate watchdog ASIC was notified of the pair's bankruptcies as early as August 2022, but chose not to act, explaining the department was limited in the "formal" investigations it could undertake.

    

    This masthead revealed in January that both men were declared bankrupt in South Africa, a status that prevents them from operating companies in Australia. Since moving to Australia, the couple have been connected to two business collapses in Perth.

    

    An ASIC spokesperson told this masthead it was "aware of and assessing reports that Lenard and Christiaan Swanepoel-Trollip, who are currently listed as directors of companies in Australia, may be automatically disqualified from managing companies due to bankruptcy orders made in South Africa".

    

    There are no recorded court outcomes, convictions or adverse findings of credit against the pair.

    

    Home Affairs and the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission both declined to comment.

    

    Despite the couple's bankruptcy, corporate records show Lenard has since created two new companies in Australia – Ubuntu Support Services on February 27 and Kinnex Pty Ltd on March 6 – where he is listed as director and secretary.

    

    An Instagram account and website created for Ubuntu Support Services claims the company offers daily living support for vulnerable people, including help with showering, dressing and grooming, household tasks like cleaning and laundry, meal preparation as well as art classes.

    

    Despite the company only starting last month, the website has five five-star reviews listed, including one listed two months ago, which says: "I've been attending the Ubuntu Hub for three months now and it's changed my life ... Best decision I ever made."

    

    Meanwhile, in a hearing on March 19, the Supreme Court of Western Australia was told through Lenard's lawyer that he wanted to liquidate a further business, NDIS-funded disability provider Bila Counselling and Support Services.

    

    The hearing was in relation to proceedings brought by Lenard in December against his sister Jennifer McAlpine, who is also a Bila shareholder, alleging misuse of client information.

    

    McAlpine's lawyer Darren Pratt told the court no steps had been taken by Lenard for more than six weeks and his client wanted the case to be dismissed and to receive costs.

    

    However, Lenard's lawyer Mark Williams told the court his client would pursue an application to wind up the organisation on "just and equitable" grounds, and the future liquidator could continue the legal proceedings against McAlpine.

    

    Supreme Court Justice Matthew Howard accepted the case had been "irregularly commenced", as Lenard Swanepoel-Trollip could not act as a director of the company and therefore cannot sue on behalf of it.

    

    Howard told the court mediation was unable to proceed and vacated injunctions imposed on McAlpine in December, but adjourned the case for further applications on cost orders and dismissal.

    

    At the same time, entities linked to the network have collapsed with mounting debts.

    

    Bila Foundation Ltd, a charity Lenard has been a director of since September 16, 2023, according to a business search, entered voluntary liquidation on February 18, with Gregory Quinn appointed liquidator. Lenard's sister and mother – Jennifer McAlpine and Magreitha Trollip – are also listed as directors.

    

    ASIC documents show the corporation owes at least $245,500, including $141,000 to employees.

    

    Another related business, Bila Support Services, entered liquidation in December last year. At the time of the collapse, the company was operated by Lenard's sister, McAlpine.

    

    ASIC records also show an application was made to deregister Christiaan's company Stemineer Pty Ltd in February.

    

    Meanwhile, staff working at a care home in Gosnells that provides round-the-clock care to clients, in Perth's south-east, run by Lenard's Bila Counselling and Support Services allege they were left unpaid and without management oversight during an internal dispute between Lenard and his sister McAlpine.

    

    One staff member has successfully launched proceedings in the Industrial Magistrates Court against the company, with others preparing similar claims.

    

    A staff member who alleged they were unpaid for a month last year told this masthead they did not understand how Bila Counselling and Support Services was still operating.

    

    "We weren't delivering the top care we should have been. I don't know how they're still operating," the former staffer said.

    

    Financial issues across the network date back to at least 2022, when Lenard's business Sunshine Counselling entered creditors' voluntary liquidation, with a liquidator report alleging the company had no assets and owed an estimated $238,000 to creditors, including $85,000 in employee entitlements and $120,000 to the tax office.

    

    Lenard has strongly rejected any allegations of wrongdoing on behalf of himself and Christiaan.

    

    "I categorically deny any wrongdoing, including any allegation of fund misappropriation or phoenixing. These allegations are false," he said.

    

    "I am in the process of obtaining comprehensive legal advice across all relevant jurisdictions.

    

    "All other matters referenced are either subject to ongoing legal proceedings or have been addressed in full in my previous correspondence, which remains on record."

Headline: A helping hand for
Full Text:
Hannah's House provides vital respite for the Goebel family

    PHOTOGRAPHY: IANMUNR O

    Many children like to carry something around with them a beloved blankie, a favourite toy or an ever-present pacifier.

    For Honey Goebel, her constant companion is a bag. But it doesn't offer comfort; instead it harbours a pump that helps keeps her alive.

    The now two-year-old was born with cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome a rare genetic disease that affects around 400 people worldwidecausing fluid on the brain, heart defects, difficulty swallowing, airway collapse, and developmental delay.

    The rare disease means Honey has already undergone two lumbar punctures and the insertion of a shunt to help reduce the pressure on her brain.

    A feeding pump, about the same size as Honey, is also attached to her 23 hours a day, feeding milk directly into her intestines via a tube.

    The lifesaving device comes at a cost, with her parents Kimese and Jarek having to make sure she doesn't get tangled in her tubes, even while she is sleeping.

    "Life has been pretty rough for her," Kimese says.

    "At the moment, she's having low blood sugars every time her feed stops, so it drops into a dangerous level, which means she has to be on her feeding pump 23 hours a day.

    "It's limiting how we live our life because we have to carry this bag around with us everywhere.

    "She's starting to get around a little bit so the pump is impacting how far she can move before it tugs on her she has to have someone hovering over her to make sure she doesn't get tangled in her own tube."

    The 24 /7 monitoring at home, on top of having to drive to constant appointments with 10 specialists at Perth Children's Hospital as well as other health workers in the community left Kimese, a mum to eight, close to "breaking point".

    In-home support from Telethon beneficiary Hannah's House has allowed Kimese and Jarek to focus on being parents, rather than just her full-time carers.

    The WA not-for-profit, which offers in-home and in-community care to children with life-limiting and complex health conditions, covered the cost of sending support workers into the Goebels' home while the family were awaiting National Disability Insurance Scheme funding for respite care. This was all thanks to a pro bono program supported by Telethon.

    "I was burning out, not eating very well, wasn't sleeping at all, and advocating until I was blue in the face because I was just constantly worried about all these issues that we don't know about with Honey," Kimese says.

    "I couldn't even imagine that there was an organisation out there like this that could help families like ours.

    "Hannah's House have been a lifesaver for us, because I've got five other kids in school, and I've got to take them to their sports, and I've still got to function and cook and clean."

    Honey has also attended the Hannah's House Playtime Program, where children with complex needs can simply enjoy being kids.

    The future is unknown for Honey since her disease is so rare but Kimese is optimistic about her progress.

    "The cells in her body don't work like ours so there's no standard, linear progression, so it's hard to tell," Kimese says.

    "I feel like she's almost thriving, in a way, now that we've got some support workers coming on board.

    "Hopefully, it's just upwards from here as she gets older."

    Honey is now taking her first steps with the help of a walker and is learning how to speak to her family using sign language.

    Hannah's House chief executive Jonine Collins says the organisation has been receiving Telethon grants for 10 years, which in turn enables them to offer much-needed support to parents and families.

    "Respite care is absolutely critical for parents and carers who look after children with complex health needs 24/7 because burnout is a massive issue with many potential knock-on effects," Ms Collins says.

    "If they don't get a break, it can drastically impact their ability to safely care for their unwell child, and their other children, spark severe stress, and take a significant toll on their own health.

    "We are so grateful that, thanks to Telethon, our free respite care can offer a safety net to many families, like Honey's, significantly reducing the strain on them and easing the pressure on WA's hospital system.

    "Without the support of Telethon and the community, we worry that families who really need our help may slip through the cracks."

Headline: Schools net $5bn in disability funding
Full Text:
Over 30 per cent of SA pupils receive aid as ...

    More than one third of South Australian students receives disability assistance in schools, with payments of up to $45,000 per student for those with the most severe needs.

    Public and private schools are receiving millions of dollars annually to boost the learning of students with physical, mental and socioemotional disabilities, with the federal bill topping $5bn a year, latest figures show.

    But parents say more can be done to support their children with additional needs as kids continue to fall through the gaps of mainstream schooling and questions remain about whether the funds are being properly spent by schools.

    The latest statistics from the Nationally Consistent Collection of Data (NCCD) on children with a disability shows 30.3 per cent of students are deemed by teachers to need an adjustment in their learning in South Australia well above the 25.7 per cent national average, which itself is twice the rate of disability in children overall (around 12 per cent).

    The extra funding is allocated for students deemed by teachers and other educational professionals as needing support for physical, cognitive, sensory or social/ emotional support.

    The NCCD funds come in addition to the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

    The SA school with the highest individual funding allocation, of $4.4m, is Tyndale Christian School in Salisbury East, followed by Ngutu College, a specialist Indigenous college which receives $3.2m.

    Other leading schools with high disability federal funding include St Peter's College ($1.5m), St John's Grammar ($1.5m), Pembroke School ($1.4m) and Scotch College ($1.3m).

    The SA government was also given $111m in 2024 for disability funding, which is supplemented by state funds.

    Adelaide Year 5 student Jerzy Ashley has attended St Michael's College at Beverly since reception.

    He has cerebral palsy and complex health needs and receives both NDIS and NCCD funding.

    Mum Emma Ashley said it meant her son could receive extra support to adjust lessons, attend camps and perform in the school musical.

    "He has initially faced barriers and challenges ... but he has had incredible support as well," she said.

    "He's had certain teachers and education support officers that have gone above and beyond to make sure that he is included. And it means that he's meaningfully taking part in school life."

    Ms Ashley, 45, believed there were "probably more kids at schools that don't have a (disability) diagnosis who need extra support".

    While a diagnosis helps secure funding, it is not necessary.

    Teachers and other classroom professionals use their professional judgment to determine the level of support needed.

    Children and Young People with Disability Australia CEO Skye Kakoschke-Moore said parents needed to know the funding doesn't work like an individual funding package and being included in the data doesn't automatically mean a child will receive a specific level of resourcing.

    However, parents had a right to be involved in conversations with educators about "reasonable adjustments, learning plans, and how their child is being supported dayto-day," she said.

Headline: Fire danger period set to end after Easter
Full Text:
Mansfield CFA captain urges caution despite early end to fire restrictions

    The Fire Danger Period within the majority of the North East including Mansfield shire will officially end on Easter Tuesday, 7 April, almost a month earlier than anticipated after what has been an exceptionally busy fire season.

    Mansfield, Wangaratta, Benalla, Alpine, Indigo, Towong, Wodonga council areas, and Alpine resorts have been included under the lifting of the fire restrictions.

    CFA Deputy Chief Officer for the North East, Gavin Thompson, said the easing of restrictions was due to a number of favourable factors within the CFA District 23 and 24 areas.

    "Recent fires in these areas have shown less intensity due to some recent welcomed rainfall," he said.

    "Rain has fallen consistently, as predicted in the region which is allowing us to ease restrictions."

    Strathbogie and Moira shires fire restrictions were lifted earlier on 30 March.

    CFA is urging residents to remain alert as the current and continued conditions can still lead to fast-moving grassfires even in cooler weather.

    Mansfield Fire Brigade CFA captain David Mims reiterated the same concerns for residents and visitors in our area.

    "With a drier than average autumn expected, the lifting of fire restrictions does not mean people should become complacent," said Mr Mims.

    "You should still monitor conditions if suitable to burn off and remember to register your burn.

    "When the fire restrictions are lifted people tend to get excited, but you have all winter to wait for the right conditions to burn off."

    If smoke or fire is reported, it will be cross-checked with the register to avoid an emergency response.

    Burn-offs can be registered online atwww.firepermits.vic.gov.auor by calling1800 668 511.

    Where possible, landowners should also notify neighbours and those nearby who may be sensitive to smoke.

    Some smoke may be visible in the district, but this is strictly for farmers such as professional seed growers to burn stubble who are exempt from the fire restriction period and are experienced and prepared in minimising risk according to the CFA.

    Mr Mims stressed it is important that when burning off for all of us that there is an adequate supply of water close by and not left unattended.

    The Easter break usually attracts many campers to the area and unfortunately brings the "usual silly behaviour" around camp fires, he said.

    "A camp fire can only be lit for cooking and warmth, it must be small and confined, not a huge bonfire."

    Campers are responsible for ensuring any camp fires are fully extinguished before leaving.

    Cross agency surveillance of the camping areas by Forest Management, DEECA and Victoria Police will be supporting the local fire brigades to ensure campers are complying with the fire season regulations during the Easter break said Mr Mims.

    The Mansfield Fire Brigade conducted its review last week post the January fires which included some communication reception issues of which the CFA is well aware of, said the local captain.

    A positive was that all firefighting members came home safely and the cooperation of other emergency agencies was "very strong," Mr Mims added.

    In addition to the bushfires, it has been a busy season with call outs to assist with two vehicle accident fatalities at Tolmie and Maindample, he said.

    The heavy workload of the Merton Fire Brigade was also noted as its members were on duty 24 hours each day during and after the bushfires which impacted properties in their area.

    "As we head into the cooler months there are several important tasks that residents should be attending to," said Mr Mims.

    "The first one is to replace the batteries in any smoke alarms in the home when daylight saving ends on 5 April 2026.

    "Another important job is the cleaning of flues and chimneys to prevent any fire risk.

    "The quality of wood makes an impact if not properly dried and can leave deposits.

    "While the immediate threat of bushfires has been greatly reduced, residents are also urged to review their evacuation plans with family members and establish an emergency meeting place before summer," Mr Mims said.

Headline: Christchurch hangs out fibre assets carrot
Full Text:
Australian infrastructure investors could soon get their hands on another lucrative offering across the Tasman, with sources suggesting that Macquarie Capital has been tapped for a possible $NZ1bn ($830m) fibre-asset sale.

    Macquarie is understood to have been hired to investigate whether to sell $NZ1bn of council-owned fibre assets in Christchurch.

    DataRoom understands that the Australian listed investment bank and an accounting firm are working on a scoping study for Enable Networks.

    It comes as Australian boutique Greenhill also carries out scoping work to assess a potential sale for the New Zealand land registry.

    Enable Networks is owned by Christchurch City Holdings Limited, the wholly owned investment arm of Christchurch City Council, which holds shares in six trading companies.

    The trading companies, known as CCTOs, or Councilcontrolled trading organisations, own and run some of the key infrastructure of Christchurch, including electricity delivery, the port, the airport, its fibre network, a4.7nd recycling facilities.

    CCHL's subsidiary companies was independently valued at over $NZ4.7bn in June 2026 and has a Standard and Poor's credit rating of AA negative outlook.

    Enable Networks was last valued at $NZ714m but sources believe the business could sell for close to $NZ1bn.

    In its interim 2026 report, CCHL said it may review its portfolio as it looked at ways to fund a potential expansion of the Lyttleton Port to support regional growth.

    It confirmed it was currently conducting an ownership review of Enable Networks. However, any move to sell assets would only come with an approval from the Christchurch City Council.

    Enable owns and operates the ultra-fast broadband fibre network across greater Christchurch and parts of Waimakariri and Selwyn districts.

    It generated $NZ128m in revenue for the year to June and $NZ41m net profit.

    Australian investors including Igneo Infrastructure Partners lined up for Kiwi fibre assets on the market last year, when electricity business Vector placed assets on the block through Barrenjoey.

    Igneo owns New Zealand business, Tuatahi First Fibre.

    Connexa, the group that owns the mobile towers of NZ telco Spark and is owned by Canadian pension funds, CDPQ and Ontario Teachers also looked.

    The assets are yet to be sold. It's worth remembering that New Zealand councils have form when it comes to voting down plans to sell assets.

    Auckland Council voted down a proposal to sell its 18 per cent holding in the listed Auckland Airport before a revised deal gained approval to sell 7 per cent in the infrastructure business.

    The cash strapped Dunedin Council also voted down a plan to sell its Aurora Energy business, first floated to pay down debt.

    The cash strapped Wellington City Council also voted down a proposal to sell a 34 per cent stake in the Wellington International Airport. However, other lucrative infrastructure opportunities could be emerging soon across the Tasman.

    Investment bank Citi is advising the New Zealand government on options for future toll road and transport development sales that could help pay for billions of dollars' worth of infrastructure, including a second Auckland harbour crossing.

    Citi's mandate will involve exploring toll road concessions on future projects, which will appeal to groups like the Australian listed Transurban. This includes The Roads of National Significance funded by the government aimed at enhancing the country's infrastructure and boosting economic growth.

    The government aims to start work on the list of 17 proposed roading projects for the program over the next two years.

Headline: $5bn handed out in disability funding to schools
Full Text:
Up to one in three Australian students now receive disability assistance in schools, with payments of up to $45,000 per student for those with the most severe needs.

    Public and private schools are receiving millions of dollars annually to boost the learning of students with physical, mental and socioemotional disabilities, with the federal bill topping $5bn a year, the latest figures show.

    Geelong schools receiving larger allocations of disability funding include Geelong Christian Education Association (Covenant College), which received $2m in 2024, and Christian College Geelong ($1.9m).

    The latest figures on the Nationally Consistent Collection of Data (NCCD) on children with a disability shows that in Victoria 27.2 per cent of students receive disability help in schools.

    That compares with the national average of 25.7 per cent and 30.3 per cent in SA, 25.9 per cent in NSW, 23.6 per cent in the ACT and Queensland, 23.5 per cent in WA and 21.8 per cent in Tasmania.

    Students in the Northern Territory are the highest overall, with 32.9 per cent receiving disability adjustments, but its demographic makes it hard to compare with other states.

    But parents say more can be done to support children with additional needs as kids continue to fall through the gaps of mainstream schooling.

    Extra funding is allocated for students categorised by teachers and other professionals as needing support for physical, cognitive, sensory or social/emotional support.

    NCCD funds come in addition to the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

    Funding is allocated according to supplementary need ($6076 for primary and $5999 for secondary), substantial need ($21,122 for primary and $21,089 for secondary) and extensive ($45,137 for primary and $45,086 for secondary).

    Schools often pool the funding, even though it is received on the basis of individual need.

Headline: Chalmers says budget will deliver reform
Full Text:
War in the Middle East and skyrocketing petrol prices will not stop Jim Chalmers delivering an ambitious fifth federal budget, with the Treasurer vowing no retreat from a fiscal blueprint aiming to deliver economic resilience and reform.

    Amid growing expectations the Albanese government could pull back from ambitious tax changes such as scaling back negative gearing and capital gains tax breaks, Chalmers told this masthead the government could not ignore the fallout from international events.

    He moved to frame his budget as one that will take on the short-term challenges faced by the global economy, as well as the long-term intergenerational challenges.

    Economists warned yesterday the savings from a 26-a-litre cut to fuel excise tax could be wiped out within weeks as the global oil price continues to climb into the foreseeable future, regardless of when the Iran war ends.

    Petrol is at record highs, reaching an average $2.58 a litre yesterday in Sydney and Melbourne, while crude oil remains around $US107 a barrel. The Albanese government announced on Monday it would halve the 52-per-litre tax on fuel for three months, starting today.

    The treasurer told this masthead the budget would be carefully calibrated to global economic conditions and would place a ''premium on what's right for the times and consistent with our ambitions and obligations to the future''.

    ''There will be a focus on intergenerational issues, and new efforts to boost productivity, find savings and lift the speed limit of our economy,'' he said.

    ''Just how difficult the economic circumstances and just how ambitious the budget will be, will be determined over the course of the next six weeks,'' he added, saying the ''extreme degree of international uncertainty'' made the task more difficult.

    Opposition Leader Angus Taylor promised he would have more to say in his budget reply about how to fix the economy, noting only that ''Labor has completely failed. Young Australians, older Australians, middle-aged Australians. They failed everybody. Because this is an economy where it's impossible to get ahead.'' Chalmers cautioned yesterday that the excise cut would not immediately show up at the petrol pump, noting it would take up to a fortnight to fully work its way through.

    But AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said it was now likely the price of Brent crude, a global benchmark, would hit US$150 a barrel, even if the war ended now and regular trading for the Middle East resumed immediately.

    ''The longer this drags on, the more oil prices globally will start to reflect the full impact of the supply hit, which means you could end up towards $US150 a barrel,'' he said.

    The price hike would be driven by the cost of repairing damaged infrastructure and the weeks it would take to bring production back to capacity.

    Oliver said if the oil price hit $US150 a barrel in coming weeks, unleaded petrol would sell for about $2.80 in Australia. However, he said prices could rise even higher if the conflict drags on.

    A rule of thumb for fuel prices is that for every $10 increase in the price of oil, petrol prices rise 10 at the bowser. ''We seem to be pushing back towards that level now and while we have a way to go yet. Potentially [barrels will cost] $US200,'' Oliver said.

    Analyst firm Wood Mackenzie said weeks more of halted exports could push Brent higher than $US200 a barrel, and financial adviser RBC Capital markets said yesterday prices were set to rise unless shipping resumed.

    ''Despite Brent pushing as high as $US115 a barrel, we believe there is still considerable room to run for prices in an extended war scenario,'' RBC said in a note to investors.

Headline: Bond markets flag a new, dangerous phase of energy shock
Full Text:
For five weeks, Iran and the United States have been trading missiles and drones. Now they're trading ... financial advice?

    After a classic Donald Trump social media post to start the trading week on Wall Street hey, we are really close to a deal, but also we might bomb Iran's power and water supplies the speaker of Iran's parliament hit back with a message for investors.

    ''Heads-up: Pre-market so-called 'news' ... is often just a set-up for profittaking,'' Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in his own post. ''Basically, it's a reverse indicator. Do the opposite: if they pump it, short it. If they dump it, go long.'' And that's broadly how Monday night's session played out on equity markets. The S&P 500 started the day positively, as investors hoped Trump's call for peace was right. Then it slowly sank into the red, as it became clear there was little break in the hostilities, and the best we could hope for on the peace front is more talk about holding talks.

    The Nasdaq tech index was again the big loser, falling 0.8 per cent, sinking further into correction territory. The magnificent seven tech stocks have become a teddy bears' picnic.

    Microsoft and Meta Platforms are both down 33 per cent from their record highs last year. Tesla, Amazon, Alphabet and Nvidia are down about 20 per cent or more.

    This is sparking some brave calls for buying, including from the likes of hedge fund billionaire Bill Ackman. He took to social media to declare ''some of the highest quality businesses in the world are trading at extremely cheap prices''.

    ''Ignore the MSM [mainstream media]. One of the most one-sided wars in history that will end well for the US and the world. And we have the potential for a large peace dividend,'' said Ackman. ''One of the best times in a long time to buy quality. Ignore the bears.'' Maybe Ackman is right. US and global earnings estimates for this calendar year suggest the war will have little effect on profits, although a big chunk of those about 40 per centwill be generated by the same tech sector that's now on the nose.

    Further, buying dips is a tried and true strategy for solid returns in the future, save for when a recession breaks out.

    And that's the big issue investors are starting to wrestle with.

    The most important move on financial markets on Monday night was in the bond market, where US Treasury yields fell sharply after US Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell said the central bank would need to weigh the energy shock in its rates deliberations.

    Blindingly obvious, yes, but it was taken as a sign that the rate cuts that had previously been ruled out may be back on the agenda. The benchmark US 10-year yield fell to 4.342 per cent, down from 4.439 per cent on Friday.

    But if the Fed is forced to cut rates, it will be doing so because the US and global economies are facing a growth shock caused by surging energy prices. The price of US oil, called West Texas crude, settled above $US100 a barrel for the first time since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. What crude prices and bond markets may be signalling is that we've entered a new phase of this energy shock.

    Paola Rodriguez-Masiu, chief oil analyst at Rystad Energy, said one reason oil prices had not risen further than they had in the first month of the war was that the buffers in the systempre-war surpluses, successful reallocation of barrels already on the water and the release of government reserves had held relatively well.

    ''But the system that held for four weeks is no longer the system we are operating in today,'' she said.

    Surging prices of refined oil products such as jet fuel (which has doubled in a month), diesel and petrol have obviously grabbed the most attention. But serious supply shortages are now creating genuine shocks in a wide range of sectors, from fertilisers and chemicals to aluminium.

    As Bloomberg columnist and energy guru Javier Blas says, demand and supply are now so out of sync that demand destruction will and must start, and governments are best to try to get ahead of this through measures that minimise the hit to economies: lower speed limits, less use of heating and cooling, and yes gulp working from home.

    That sudden switch in US bond markets we saw on Monday nightfrom expecting rate increases to anticipating rate cuts tells us that some parts of financial markets are already expecting this demand destruction to worsen. And it won't be pretty.

    All of which makes the Albanese's government's decision to cut the fuel excise a curious one. The logic might be hard to fault from a political perspective. But it helps maintain demand for fuel in the Australian economy at a time when we really need it to fall.

    By contrast, Chanticleer's train into the office on Tuesday morning in Melbourne was packed after the Victorian government decided to make public transport free for a month. That looks to be a sensible approach to managing demand and providing costof-living relief.

    In a way, the Albanese government is taking a bet informed by lots of good market intelligence and data, no doubtthat this war will be done and dusted in a relatively short time. It's the same bet the market has been making since the war began. And it gets riskier by the day.

Headline: Officer's truck chaos
Full Text:
Cardinia Shire streets are under strain as hundreds of trucks rumble through Officer daily, sparking safety and noise concerns among locals.

    Around 200 trucks are reportedly entering Browns, Bayview, and Pecks roads each day, delivering soil to private properties.

    One site has been completed, while work continues at a second location near Browns Road and Godfrey Lane, where residents claim traffic controls and site facilities are lacking.

    Locals report speeding trucks, dust, congestion, and near misses, with council allegedly receiving around 50 complaints. Patricia Clarke is worried about trucks flouting the 60km/h limit near a Catholic primary school.

    Residents say they had little warning before works began and remain frustrated at delays, with activity ongoing for six months despite council claims the project is "finishing soon."

    They are calling for transparency about truck origins, materials, and timelines, urging council and EPA inspections.

    The EPA confirmed monitoring the site but declined further comment while investigations continue.

    STORY PAGE 3

    Trucks flooding Officer Hundreds of trucks are flooding Cardinia Shire streets daily, leaving residents worried about safety, noise, and reckless driving.

    It is believed approximately 200 trucks were travelling from the freeway each day, before entering Browns Road, Bayview Road, Pecks Road in Officer.

    Trucks were seen delivering soil to two private properties, with one site reportedly completed and work continuing at the second.

    The activity intensified at a second site near Browns Road and Godfrey Lane, where locals claim there were no visible traffic controls or site facilities.

    One neighbour said a council officer acknowledged around 50 complaints relating congestion, dust, noise, near misses and speeding.

Headline: Operation Nexus: Police target high risk Easter road users
Full Text:
RoadSafe Westgate is proud to support Operation Nexus 2026, the statewide road policing campaign led by Victoria Police ahead of the Victorian Easter holiday period.

    With increased traffic expected across metropolitan Melbourne and regional Victoria, police will launch a highly visible enforcement and education blitz aimed at preventing road trauma and saving lives.

    When is Operation Nexus 2026? Operation Arid will run from 12:01am Thursday 2 April to 11:59pm Monday 6 April, covering the entire Easter break, a traditionally high-risk period for serious and fatal crashes on Victorian roads.

    Why This Easter Holiday Matters Holiday periods mean more vehicles on the road, longer trips, unfamiliar routes and tighter travel schedules. Historically, the highest risk periods occur when drivers are: Leaving for holiday destinations Returning home Driving while fatigued Travelling at speed on freeways and regional highways Police intelligence shows that single acts of non-compliance and basic driving errors contributed to more than half of fatalities in 2025- including low-range speeding, distraction, drink driving and failure to obey road rules.

    What Police Will Be Targeting During Operation Nexus 2026, Victoria Police will focus on the driving behaviours most closely linked to deaths and serious injuries: Speeding- including low-range speeding Distracted driving- particularly illegal mobile phone use Seatbelt and child restraint offences Fatigue and drowsy driving Alcohol and drug-impaired driving Police will be highly visible across major freeways, arterial roads and regional routes.

    Senior Sergeant Stephen O'Connell, Road Policing Advisor from Westgate Highway Patrol, said "We will be out in force, both educating and enforcing. Our aim is simple: prevent lives lost and serious injuries on Victorian roads."

    He added that drivers should expect to be tested anywhere, anytime throughout the holiday period.

    A Community Responsibility Chair of RoadSafe Westgate Jim Giddings reinforced the importance of shared responsibility.

    "Speed is a factor in most serious crashes. Driving safely isn't just about obeying the law. It's about respect for yourself, your passengers, your family and the broader community."

    Road trauma does not only affect those directly involved. It impacts families, friends, emergency services and communities often for a lifetime.

    If you witness dangerous driving, report it to Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

    If you plan to have a drink then plan to not drive, taking a big risk like drinking and driving is just not worth endangering your live or that of other road users.

    Fatigue remains one of the leading contributors to serious crashes. If you are tired, stop and rest.

    Enforcement will be high. The stakes are higher.

    Speedsters and drivers who flout the road rules have been put on notice.

    This Easter break, enforcement will be visible and sustained - but the ultimate goal is not fines. It is preventing tragedy.

    Road safety is not someone else's responsibility. It is yours.

    Enjoy your Easter breakwith family and friends and travel so you arrive safely.

Headline: Homes power on
Full Text:
Hobsons Bay council has voted in support of plans for a social housing development on Power Street in Williamstown.

    At it's meeting on Tuesday 24 March, council endorsed the state government's proposal to build a five-storey complex with 65 social housing apartments on a vacant block at 5 Power Street.

    While a state government project, council voted to endorse the rezoning of the area in order for the apartments to built and also for council to write a letter in support to the community consultation process currently underway.

    Consultation on the Power Street apartments closes at the end of the month and some nearby residents have already launched a campaign to stop it.

    A Change.org petition calling on Planning Minister Sonia Kilkenny to refuse the rezoning of the area and prevent the apartments from being built has already attracted 250 signatures.

    The petitioners argue the development would increase traffic congestion, put further strain on existing infrastructure, is out of scale with neighbouring buildings and presents safety risk to children and pedestrians from the nearby train station, childcare centre and schools.

    Attempts by Star Weekly to contact the petitioners were unsuccessful.

    However, one of those to have signed the petition is local ward councillor and Hobsons Bay deputy mayor Lisa Bentley, who spoke against the plans at Tuesday night's meeting.

    "Over recent days a considerable number of residents have contacted me complaining the have not been consulted on this proposal," Cr Bentley said, adding that while social housing was vital, local residents were worried about the location and size of the Power Street proposal.

    "These concerns are being expressed respectfully, but they are genuine," she said.

    However, the mover of the motion, Cr Rayane Hawli, said Williamstown had a long history of social and public housing and that Power Street was an ideal location for more.

    "Its close proximity to public transport (North Williamstown Station) does make it a suitable location for this type of development and arguably addresses the traffic concern," Cr Hawli said, arguing the proposal had broad community support.

    "I don't believe the majority of Hobsons Bay residents believe in stigmatising those who need social housing," she said.

    "Exclusion does not make the community safer."

Headline: Transport help needed
Full Text:
Volunteer drivers are sought for Grampians Community Health's community car volunteer program, to transport people to medical appointments in major centres.

    The program has grown steadily during the past year, with more than 10 dedicated volunteers collectively providing more than 168 trips covering 41,636 kilometres.

    Volunteer co-ordinator Jane Goninon said the program delivered by Grampians Community Health was more than just numbers.

    "It's about connection and getting people to potentially critical appointments," she said.

    "Our volunteers are not just drivers they're companions, listeners and friendly faces. For many clients, it's the highlight of their week."

    Designed to support residents who face transport barriers including seniors, people with disabilities, and those undergoing medical treatment the program pairs volunteer drivers with those in need of safe, reliable transport.

    The program's fee may be subsidised by an aged-care plan, NDIS or the Victorian Patient Transport Assistance Scheme.

    The program offers flexibility, allowing volunteers to choose their availability and preferred routes. Training and support are provided, ensuring every driver feels confident and valued.

    To learn more, people can visit gch.org. au, or call Ms Goninon on 5358 7400 on Wednesdays.
