Headline: Council pushes jet ski safety crackdown
Full Text:
MORNINGTON Peninsula Shire councillors have backed a push to strengthen enforcement of jet ski regulations, voting to submit a motion to the Municipal Association of Victoria (MAV) State Council meeting in May.

    The motion calls on the state government to increase enforcement of personal watercraft rules, particularly around speed limits and safe distances from swimmers.

    Council officers said submitting a shire-led motion would elevate the issue at a state level and highlight safety concerns shared by coastal communities.

    The MAV has confirmed the issue is strategically relevant, noting its impact on community safety and amenity across Victoria's coastline.

    The Association of Bayside Municipalities has also endorsed the proposal, aligning with its strategic goal to "advocate for improved personal watercraft licencing, enforcement and education".

    Jet ski safety has been a key advocacy priority for the shire over 2025/26, following increased complaints from residents and visitors. Council said reckless behaviour, including near misses with swimmers and impacts on marine life, had become a growing concern.

    Councillors voted unanimously in support of the officer recommendation at their 17 March meeting.

    Cr Michael Stephens said stronger enforcement was critical.

    "I support the recommendation that council endorse the submission of this motion to the MAV. In recent years, I've seen increasing and consistent concerns from the community regarding the operation of watercraft, particularly jet skis, in close proximity to swimmers and wildlife," he said.

    "While regulations already exist. the key issue being raised by our community is the enforcement. Without effective enforcement, these regulations cannot provide the level of safety and reassurance that our residents expect when using our beaches."

    Stephens said the MAV submission would allow councils to "speak with a united voice" and push for "more consistent and visible enforcement of existing regulations".

    Acting mayor Cr Paul Pingiaro said the shire had already written to the Minister and highlighted recent enforcement efforts.

    "Operation Summer Safe led to over 100 infringements 1n a very short period," he said.

    He also stressed the importance of education around rules, including speed limits near swimmers and extended 500-metre coastal restrictions between Martha Cove and Point Nepean.

    "But most of all, education so people understand that there's a change from the 200 metres to the 500 metres," >9 they said.

    He added the advocacy push includes increased police patrols, CCTV, drone monitoring, clearer signage and restrictions on jet skis entering swimming-only zones.

    "No boating zones mean no boating. That's jet skis included."

    Cr David Gill said enforcement remained the biggest challenge due to limited resources.

    Policing is the difficult part; enforcement is the difficult part. .. it's just a financial impediment at the moment.i If supported at the MAV State Council's 29 May meeting, the motion would strengthen advocacy efforts and increase pressure on the state government to act.

Headline: Morwell blanketed in thick fog
Full Text:
FROM fog to storm, the Latrobe Valley experienced a wide range of weather conditions last week.

    Last Tuesday (March 24), locals woke up to a foggy morning and drifted into a warm day, reaching a top of 29 degrees, creating a perfect combination for a summer storm.

    About 8.4 millimetres of rain was recorded in the Latrobe Valley on Tuesday, with major rainfall hitting around 4.30pm and again at 9.30pm.

    Throughout the night the storm eased, with Wednesday (March 25) morning opening up to a fog-filled morning, leading to a warm storm evening.

    Rain was forecasted for Tuesday and Wednesday, with up to 16mm predicted by the Bureau of Meteorology, with a further 30mm on Thursday (March 26) and Friday (March 27).

    According to BoM's daily weather observations, about 16mm of rain was recorded from Tuesday to Friday.

    Latrobe missed the mass of the weather event, with Ladner Park's 2026 Farm World getting the brunt of the rain in waves.

    Authorities warn that drivers should put their lights on in foggy mornings to ensure that other drivers can see their vehicles, as well as taking extra precaution on the road to avoid incidents.

    On the outskirts of Gippsland, the Mt Hotham Alpine Resort was already reporting snow last Saturday (March 28).

    Winter has come early in some places, while others are still seeing temperatures in the high 20s.

    With a dedicated family of Coordinators, Care Managers and Support Workers, After-Care delivers services to all of Southeast Melbourne, as far as Ringwood.

    When you choose After-Care to provide your services, you will get: Individualised support. tailored to your personal preferences and needs A dedicated Care Manager who will visit you in your home and learn about you as a person Support Workers who are fully trained and uphold the After-Care family values Support when you need it.

Headline: Callout to blood donors
Full Text:
Australian Red Cross Lifeblood is urgently calling on Colac and district residents with type O and A blood to donate, with reserves under extreme pressure this Easter.

    While Colac does not have a donor centre and relies on a mobile van visiting intermittently during the year, the city's closest donor centres are at Geelong, Ballarat and Warrnambool.

    Lifeblood urged eligible donors to book now and donate as close to home as possible this Easter to boost the organisation's blood supply.

    There are 5000 extra donations needed in Victoria until April 10 to ensure blood is available for people injured in accidents and emergencies, as well as for thousands of other seriously ill patients.

    Lifeblood donor experience executive director Cath Stone said while donations surged after the Bondi attack, appointments had dipped in the lead-up to Easter.

    "The need for blood continues well beyond any single event. Blood is needed every day, and demand can spike around Easter due to increased road accidents and ongoing cancer treatment needs, at a time when many regular donors take a break," she said.

    Ms Stone said while O-negative blood was vital in emergencies because it could be given to any patient when their blood type is unknown, O-positive was increasingly used as a critical back-up.

    Plasma donations are also in demand, accounting for around half of all donations needed this Easter long weekend.

    Donations are especially needed on Good Friday, with many donor centres opening across Victoria and operating across the entire long weekend.

    People can book a donation by visiting Lifeblood's website, using the app or calling 13 14 95.

Headline: Construction begins on major student tower at 570 Little Bourke St
Full Text:
Construction has officially begun on a major new student accommodation tower at 570 Little Bourke St, with project partners marking the milestone at a ground-breaking and time capsule ceremony in the CBD on March 23.

    The $300 million purpose-built student accommodation project will deliver 892 beds across 748 units in a 26-level building, making it one of the largest student housing developments to commence in the CBD in recent years. UniLodge has also been confirmed as the operator, with students expected to move in for semester one, 2028.

    Representatives from Hickory, MaxCap and UniLodge were joined at the ceremony by Lord Mayor Nick Reece, former Lord Mayor Sally Capp, and representatives from RMIT University and The University of Melbourne.

    The project is being developed as a joint venture between Hickory and MaxCap, with Hickory also acting as builder. It is the first project Hickory has delivered under its integrated builder-developer model, which the company says helps reduce planning and delivery risk while providing greater certainty around construction outcomes.

    Designed by Nettletontribe, the development will include a library, gymnasium, cinema, music room, group dining areas, lounges and games spaces. The design also aims to improve a long-neglected stretch of the western CBD by reinterpreting the site's historic character and surrounding bluestone, sandstone and red brick streetscape.

    Importantly, the project will also revive the historic Great Western Hotel, introduce new retail spaces, activate the adjoining Brown Alley and improve pedestrian safety and access between Lonsdale and Little Bourke streets.

    The development forms part of a broader push by Hickory to reshape this part of the city. The company is also progressing a second major western CBD project at 580 Lonsdale St, the former Kilkenny Inn site, meaning the two developments will collectively deliver around 1250 student accommodation units while restoring two historic pubs, the Great Western Hotel and the Kilkenny Inn.

all safe. We must admit that the NDIS is not working for everybody. If we want the NDIS system to be the system it was intended to be, to truly provide security and dignity for people with a disability, the NDIS needs the structural change proposed in this bill. I say to people with a disability and their families, we have your back. We know change is frightening for participants and providers. It's particularly scary for those who rely on the NDIS every single day to have a shower, to eat fresh, healthy food, to get out into the community, to go to work, to be part of what it means to be human, to get out into the environment. I say to people with a disability and their families, we will walk with you and we are listening. We are committed to ensuring the NDIS delivers essential supports to Australians with significant and permanent disability, not just today but for generations to come. I am incredibly proud to be a member of the Labor Party, a member of a party who introduced this incredible scheme that has transformed the lives of people with a disability and their families right across the across the country. story_title: Parliament Passes New Laws Targeting NDIS Fraud and Misconduct
story_summary: The Australian Parliament has passed the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment Integrity and Safeguarding Bill to combat widespread fraud, rorting, and misconduct. The new laws introduce tougher penalties, including up to five years in jail and multi-million dollar fines for providers who violate banning orders or engage in deceptive marketing. These reforms aim to give the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission stronger powers for earlier intervention, expand whistleblower protections, and better protect participants from exploitation. The government has also significantly increased the NDIS agency's workforce by nearly 2,000 employees to improve service delivery, while some parliamentarians and advocates raise concerns about potential impacts on participant rights and funding.

Any power that allows support to vulnerable individuals to be altered in what appears to be a non-transparent fashion has to be accompanied by clear limits. I would argue that it has to actually be rendered transparent and that I would it has to include an opportunity for participants to request review and appeal of those changes. Reforms that rely on discretion rather than explicit safeguards risk shifting the balance of power in any situation away from participants and towards administrative control. This is fundamentally inconsistent with the intent of the NDIS as a participant-centred insurance scheme. These concerns come into sharper focus when they're placed alongside the new icann assessment tool. In the coming months, NDIS participants will begin to be assessed using a structured interview process conducted by ndia-appointed assessors using the instrument for the classification and assessment of support. The objectives of this reform are understandable. The current system places an unfair burden on participants to gather medical evidence for assessment. That's time consuming and can be costly. It can really slow the process down. Both the independent review into the National Disability Insurance Scheme and my own personal professional experience of having worked within it for many years as a paediatric neurologist both testified to the fact that the existing system evolves inefficient, duplicative and inconsistent evidence gathering, which can on some occasions very much undermine the participant experience and can create an unusual and unreasonable workload for healthcare professionals who are trying to assist individuals in securing appropriate supports under the NDIS But as University of New South Wales researchers have pointed out, Deputy Speaker, the move to ICANN raises some pretty important questions. For example, how will assessment results translate into budget decisions for participants? What additional evidence might be considered or will be considered when medical reports are no longer required to inform the planning process? What will inform the planning process? And how will consistent, transparent and fair decisions be applied by differing assessors over time? We've seen in the past that inconsistency has been a consistent bugbear for many individuals operating within the NDIS and that individuals with very similar support needs have on many innumerable occasions received very different support packages. Now the ICANN should measure support needs across 12 areas of daily life including mobility, self-care, communication, relationships and physical and mental health. Each of those areas is scored on two scales how often support is needed and how intensive the level of support that is required is. However, reducing patients with sometimes individuals, participants with sometimes extremely complex care needs, which can sometimes be multifactorial to a single binomial score, can present some significant complexities. The reality is that a score does not reflect a lived experience and that an assessment tool is only as fair as the system that we put in place to interpret it. If we put garbage in, we will get garbage out. And we can't necessarily equitably and effectively reduce people with very complex medical and physical needs to binomial scores. We're already seeing this play out with the integrated assessment tool in the aged care system. I know that I and many of my colleagues in this place are hearing from affected individuals within the aged care system every day that tool is not working for them. So I think that we have reasonable grounds for concern, Deputy Speaker, that this similar tool may not work well within the disability space. I hope to be wrong on that, but I have some concerns regarding it. When we combine this new tool with new statutory powers to reduce support without a new assessment, there has to be a risk, whether that is intentional or not, of a new system in which reassessment outcomes and administrative discretion interact in a way that could well disadvantage NDIS participants. So I support the calls of people with a disability Australia for stronger protections, specifically their recommendation that plain language reasons for decision making and that administrative review tribunal review rights be required where plan variations reduce the total funding that recipients are receiving and that all recipients should be able to access independent advocacy when they need to contest such decisions. It's only fair. It's only reasonable. reasonable. I urge the minister and the National Disability Insurance Agency to approach the implementation of these changes with the sort of care that, wherever practicable, will err on the side of participant protection. NDIS reform which focuses support on functional needs, which builds strong foundational supports and which addresses waste and exploitation to preserve resources for those who rely on them is critically important. All of us in this place recognise that. As a former participant within the system and now someone who has from this place sought to improve it, I have been supportive of changes in that respect and of this nature in the past. But I've always been clear in my previous professional life and in this one that those reforms can't erode the rights of participants. The independent NDIS review and the Disability Royal Commission have both found and emphasised that trust in the scheme depends on its transparency, its fairness and its accountability. That means participants need should and deserve to know when decisions can be changed, on what basis and how they can challenge such decisions. The NDIS only exists because Australia has made a collective commitment, a significant collective commitment, that people who are living with a disability will not be left to navigate fragmented or inadequate systems alone. That commitment will not end, it should not end, it cannot end, simply because it's become too complicated or too costly to deliver on it. The bill before the House contains measures which do strengthen the NDIS but it also contains others that place significant weight, perhaps too much weight, on administrative discretion without sufficiently explicit safeguards. As these changes are are implemented the government has to continue to engage closely with all parts of the sector to ensure that these reforms do not affect participant dignity, fairness or access. Above all else, the people who access the NDIS have to remain at the centre of it. Full Text: And so within that growth, the changes that the government is making through this legislation, but as part of its wider plan, is, I think, reinforcement, getting back to what I said to begin with, very pleased to see that the opposition has that long-term optimism in the success of the NDIS There are a couple of features of this bill that I think are really worth emphasising. One is the promotions order. I know that some of the things I'm about to mention here are probably illegal anyway and already would be caught up in the law as it is. But this is the sort of extent that some providers will go to get business. Now, these are both anecdotal stories, but one was from a very good source, from a a local Indigenous health service, in fact, who said that there are now providers literally trawling through supermarkets in Logan, literally going through the train station, looking for obviously vulnerable people and trying to sign them up to the NDIS or trying to sign them up as part of their plan. Absolutely disgraceful. But again, anecdotally, this one may be not as good a source as that first one, but stories of cashbacks. Providers offering cashbacks if you sign up to the NDIS Unfortunately, it's believable. And it's believable when you realise that some providers see a participant as a prize cow. That somebody with a million dollar plan is really treated as just this, you know, as prize cattle. Which is incidentally incidentally a concept that fundamentally undermines choice and control, which is supposed to be at the heart of the NDIS That if your plan is seen as not profitable for the needs they'll need to provide, you won't be able to get a provider. So what sort of choice and control is that when you're not actually able to choose your provider because the provider doesn't see you as profitable enough. The other thing I'd just say on fraud is that there are... It is probably the central problem that the community sees with the NDIS is fraud. And I think the thing to really say about that, and this is where I think the opposition... This probably is the best example of how the opposition just completely took their hands off the wheel, is that this government is now reviewing more claims every single day for fraud than the previous government reviewed in a year. It is almost unbelievable to think that is possible. And it took investment. It took an investment in systems and it took an investment in people. Perhaps it was just this ideological obsession with not employing public servants and outsourcing and trying to cut costs. I mean, we saw it in so many areas, whether it was 41,000 veterans waiting for their claims to be processed when we came to government, whether it was the robo-debt and the heartache that was Centrelink. The NDIA also suffered that. And so I think that just is absolutely worth underlining. That's a stunning figure that we review more claims every single day than the previous government reviewed in an entire year. And so I think that at the heart of this, government and this party was responsible for the birth of the NDIS Unfortunately, we weren't there while it turned into a delinquent teenager, but we're back now. And I think at the heart of this government's approach is what the disability community says which is that nothing about us without us. That this approach that we are taking is something that we are working in lockstep with people from the disability community who this affects. And I think that is something which is the Labor way, and it is unsurprising that it is only the Labor Party that is actually able to fix the NDIS and to get it back on track. And so I commend the bill to the House. As I say, I'm pleased, despite the politicking that goes on, to know that the opposition, in their heart, want to see it work, because I think in the Australian community, we want to see it work as well. But it's going to take a lot of effort, and it's going to take a lot of us working together to make it happen. This is not the beginning of the process of fixing it, but it is an important step on the way. There is a lot more to be done, and I commend this to the House. The question now is that the member be agreed to, and I call the member for Cooyong. Thank you very much Deputy Speaker. The NDIS the National Disability Insurance Scheme is one of Australia's most significant social reforms. And while the significance of the NDIS means that we have to protect its ongoing financial sustainability, it's important that we in this place always remember that reforms must not come at the expense of participants' rights, their fairness, dignity or access, and that all changes to the NDIS have to strengthen the scheme for the long term, whilst keeping those who access it and whose lives depend upon it firmly at the centre of any changes to its design. This bill contains measures that respond to real and serious problems which confront the NDIS Strengthening the powers of the NDIS Quality and Safety Safeguards Commission to detect abuse, to prevent exploitation and enforce accountability are important and overdue measures. This bill also strengthens the framework to ensure fit-for-purpose penalties and offences that should deter providers from doing the wrong thing and which should also ensure that unsuitable people can be excluded from providing services under the auspices of the NDIS Deputy Speaker, NDIS participants have to be kept safe by our system and providers who do the wrong thing must face consequences. This bill will help instal some of those guardrails. But it's concerning that this bill also gives the chief executive officer of the ndia the ability to vary a participant's plan, including increasing or decreasing the total funding amount available under both the old and new framework plans. This power can be exercised unless the act or the NDIS rules expressly provide otherwise, and it can be exercised without need for a reassessment. The explanatory memorandum for this bill states that this amendment codifies for the absence of of doubt what is actually an existing practise within the agency. It is described as a clarification rather than a change in the substance of how the NDIA operates. The explanatory memorandum further claims that these changes do not impact or change the circumstances in which the CEO can vary a participant's plan. But I have to note that for participants, for advocates and for Australians in the broader disability community, this change feels consequential. Their very justifiable concern is not that plans can occasionally be adjusted. There are clearly circumstances in which increases to total funding amounts are essential. The concern is that this amendment codifies the power to single-handedly reduce supports without a fresh assessment of participants and without the sorts of procedural safeguards that participants should reasonably be able to expect when their support funding is at stake. Advocates who participated in the Senate inquiry into this bill also expressed the reasonable concern that this provision could be used in ways which are actively harmful or which could have unintended consequences, particularly if and when participants are not involved or consulted in variations to their plan. We have to remember that people whose independence and whose well-being rely on stability of support, for those individuals an NDIS plan is not an abstract budget. It can be the difference between being able to live at home or not. It can be the difference between experiencing consistency and security of care or experiencing a personal crisis.

story_title: Parliament Passes New Laws Targeting NDIS Fraud and Misconduct
story_summary: The Australian Parliament has passed the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment Integrity and Safeguarding Bill to combat widespread fraud, rorting, and misconduct. The new laws introduce tougher penalties, including up to five years in jail and multi-million dollar fines for providers who violate banning orders or engage in deceptive marketing. These reforms aim to give the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission stronger powers for earlier intervention, expand whistleblower protections, and better protect participants from exploitation. The changes come amid criticism of the scheme being a 'honeypot' for organised crime and concerns over its unsustainable cost growth, which is projected to reach $50 billion. The government has also significantly increased the NDIS agency's workforce by nearly 2,000 employees to improve service delivery, while some parliamentarians and advocates raise concerns about potential impacts on participant rights and funding.

Full Text:
Interview
A new report has found that 50% of Australians are avoiding healthcare they need because care they need because they can't afford it. The report by the Consumers Health Forum sheds light on entrenched inequities in the health system, noting that Australians living with disability, chronic illness or who are of diverse backgrounds are more likely to miss out on care. Jeremy Hope is the President of People with Disability Australia, the national advocacy group for people living with a disability and he joins us now from Canberra. Jeremy Hope, welcome. So this survey found so many Australians are missing out on health care because of cost. How acute are the challenges for people with disability in particular?
Yeah, hi, thank you. It's extremely acute. The over-representation, disproportionate of people living with disability that are living with cost barriers and with impact and having to make decisions on do I go to work, do I buy food, do I go and see a doctor is considerable and quite alarming that it might happen. And our concern is cost of living with that barrier now increasing. We see it every day with the news and the groceries, et cetera, that making critical decisions has an impact on daily life. And that impact on daily life has a ripple effect that can lead to hospitalisations, can lead to impact on greater resource heavy loads on the NDIS that is already over servicing. So the difficulty there on the need, our concern is that people will have to make horrible decisions and left at risk out of fear and out of not deciding what to do.
The National Disability Insurance Scheme was welcomed in Australia as a landmark system to help people with disability. How is that figuring now in the ability of people with disability to access healthcare?
I think the ability to access health care is that people that have got access to the NDIS are fortunate enough that they can access supports to help with transportation and to help get to appointments. The difficulty is getting that appointment and being able to afford the appointments. NDIS pay for support and a support person to help people access. They don't pay for the cost of medical bills like a GP if they need to pay out of pocket or if they're needing to pay for psychology, psychiatrists or even medications that we take for granted. All of that is normal out of day, everyday use and although we're grateful, people with disability on NDIS is only a small proportion of people with disability and a lot of people go to work every day with a disability, earn a wage, a living, pay taxes but are still impacted by not having enough funds to go and get those necessities they need. What about the Government saying it slashed the cost of medicines on the PBS and expanded bulk billing? Look, I acknowledge and we're grateful for bulk billing and the access to doctors. I think talking about access to doctors, a lot of clinics are not accessible. So finding a clinic that is accessible, finding a clinic with an appointment available that's got an appointment. I've got a daughter with a disability. Her doctor was away. It took a month to be able to see a doctor, to get prescriptions prescribed, to see, and that resulted in hospitalisation and more imposts, just for one there. I think the difficulty there with PBS although there's Grateful, some medications are not on PBS And again, if I use an example that's personal, I've got a daughter on a disability pension that is paying over $300 a month in medications and that's not affordable on the pension when you're covering your everyday pay. So even, you mentioned your personal experience there, even in a city like Canberra, it took you a month to get an appointment and prescriptions? Yeah, I'm visiting Canberra, but I live in Western Sydney, and to be able to see someone that understands my lived experience, my daughter's disability, someone that she feels safe to go to, be able to treat some of those chronic illnesses that are needed.
We weren't able to meet that need.
And so we've got a budget coming up. Have you got any special requests of Jim Chalmers going into that budget period considering the particular challenges?
Look, obviously we definitely welcome the extended PBS relief and access to medications. Bulk billing is definitely needed. But access and being able to think about bricks and mortar and how do we, is the building accessible, is it safe for people with sensory needs like autism etc. Are doctors informed and trained to deal with a range and a vast of disabilities and be able to work through I think some of those those elements but definitely the access and the availability of doctors is something that is needed hospitals are there and i think some of the difficulties is with the ripple effect of not being able to see doctors and specialists with people being fearful of going to doctors because of that out-of-pocket or they might not buy their medication because they need to buy food for the family the ripple effect is going to be on hospitals as well and so I think the difficulty is looking, we need to look at how we support people with disability holistically, not just on the NDIS but their whole of life and their whole journey of life. And so that is accessing work, accessing supports, and also going to the doctors, having food that is affordable, having relief and being able to afford to run a car or have access to public transport. All of that helps an individual be able to live a whole and independent life. Okay, Jeremy Hope, thanks so much for talking to us from Canberra.
Yeah, appreciate that, Joe. Thank you.

The original question was that this bill be now read a second time. To this, the honourable member for Lindsay has moved as an amendment that all words after that be omitted with a view to substituting other words. The question now is that the amendment be agreed to and I call the Member for Ford. On the question that the amendment be agreed to?
So I rise in support of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment Integrity and Safeguarding Bill 2025 and in doing, I acknowledge the contribution of the member for Lindsay and appreciate that speaking for the the opposition there, I do appreciate the depth of support that you expressed in your speech there for the NDIS and your desire for for it to be sustainable. And so I want to acknowledge that. Of course, there are some things in that speech, Deputy Speaker, that I think also need to be addressed. And one is that when the opposition talk about it growing unsustainably today, I think it sort of needs to be pointed out that when we came to government, it was growing at about 22%, totally unsustainable. After they oversaw its implementation from the trial period until we got into government, I think we really saw it being completely mismanaged, both in terms of the number of growth, but something else which the member for Lindsay said there, that we now have a scheme with about 720,000 people on it. In Queensland, I know when the productivity was first designed in the NDIS it was was designed for somewhere around 95,000 Queenslanders. But in effect, we've ended up with somewhere around 175,000 Queenslanders.
So totally unsustainable at those levels. And I think that I'd like to acknowledge really the work that Senator McAllister, the Minister and the Health Minister have done recently to get the NDIS back on track.
I'd also like like to acknowledge the work that the former Minister Bill Shorten also did. I mean, somebody I think who is perhaps more responsible for anybody than anybody else for actually the beginning of the scheme was unfortunately witness to it being so badly managed while Labor was in opposition. And I think the work that he did when we got back into government in 2022 really has begun to get it back on track. You know, we are headed to that short-term target of an 8% growth, down from 22%. But many of the things that Memphil Lindsay talked about, there not being a plan, there absolutely is a plan. And it's being rolled out now. Unfortunately, being rolled out, well, the scheme is as big as it is when it could have been dealt with at the time. And so it is pleasing to hear the opposition talk positively about their attitude to the NDIS and the future of the NDIS because it is a scheme that Australians rightly should be proud of. It is a world-leading scheme and it changes people's lives for the better in a way that would have been unconceivable in the past. In fact, I remember being a young staffer to Peter Duncan, the former member for Macon in the 90s, and one memory, more than almost any other memory that sticks with me was visiting community centres where there were parents with disabled kids just desperate for any assistance that they could get. And the emotion that I felt on those visits is something that has stayed with me for decades. And talking to families who were involved in Disability Services Queensland, it is worlds apart with what the NDIS is, with all of its flaws, compared to what it was like when it was through Disability Services Queensland. And I should say that, and I just want to say, you know, I'm no political professional. I feel like I need to make this point before I go on to my next point. No political professional. I, you know, ran a construction company, worked on the land. But then I found myself working for a senator in 2018, Senator Murray Watt, doing most of his, in fact, all of his constituent work, all of the electorate work. And in 2018, where we saw the NDIS go from a trial to being fully implemented. And we began to have a trickle of complaints coming into the electorate office. And one story that I remember really stands out from that time that a severely disabled child, an autistic child, was trying to get an assistance dog and the dog cost 20 grand or something like that. They're not cheap. So the NDIA approved $5,000 worth of reports, OTs, psychologists, whatever, and then another $2,000 for support coordination to get those reports together. So $7,000 in total for reports, which is ludicrous in itself, because the family duly went away and the professionals said, yes, this child would benefit from a dog of reasonable and necessary support. Ludicrous in itself that it should be $7,000 to get it, but guess what the ndia said when it got the reports? No dog. Denied the... I mean, if it wasn't true, it would indeed be funny. funny. And so this family then began the journey that so many families undertake, which is going through the review process, going to the aat, fighting the agency all the way, the agency fighting tooth and nail back then. And I remember it was during covid because the family got to the night before the hearing. And this is where the agency had spent $7,000 on the reports, potentially tens of thousands of dollars on a top-tier legal firm to fight this family all the way to the night before the hearing, where they even got the covid test so that they could go and attend the hearing the next day. The agency caved caved in and gave them the dog. And so it is those sorts of stories which we saw in 2018 to 2020 that on a personal level, turned me off the NDIS so much that in my own family, we've got a family member who's autistic that needs a bit of help, but I thought taking part in those decisions about whether or not we pursue the NDIS I thought that it was actually the supports that they would get through the NDIS would not be worth the hassle that it would take for them to go through the process process of applying and then fighting for supports. Of course, now we know that there are no other services that exist outside the NDIS They've all been been allowed to die on the vine.
And so the NDIS is, as it is often said, the only lifeboat in the ocean.
And now that family member is going to have to try and get some support through the NDIS But it was such a horror story that I witnessed there in my time in Murray's office that really turned me off even trying to get the NDIS supports for him. And now I think what we saw then was the opportunity when the scheme was beginning to tackle the problems as they arose. But instead what happened, the problems that existed then in 2018 just scaled up as the scheme scaled up. And it was, I think, left for the rest of us, not in government, to sit there and just watch it, Korean, completely out of control. And now any member in this House would know that NDIS is probably the single most biggest issue that will come to us as a constituent concern. So that trickle that we witnessed in 2018 has really turned into a flood. And there is is something that we know all along was fundamentally broken and that this government is trying to get back on track. And I think that it should be said too that because I feel like I need to be careful when I say that because the NDIS is so so life changing and so important for people that I think the message needs to be that it will continue to grow. That short term goal of an 8% growth coming into the longer term goal of 5 or 6% in line with the growth of Medicare and aged care, that it will continue to grow. People, I think, need to have faith in that.

story_title: Parliament Passes New Laws Targeting NDIS Fraud and Misconduct
story_summary: The Australian Parliament has passed the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment Integrity and Safeguarding Bill to combat widespread fraud, rorting, and misconduct. The new laws introduce tougher penalties, including up to five years in jail and multi-million dollar fines for providers who violate banning orders or engage in deceptive marketing. These reforms aim to give the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission stronger powers for earlier intervention, expand whistleblower protections, and better protect participants from exploitation. The changes come amid criticism of the scheme being a 'honeypot' for organised crime and concerns over its unsustainable cost growth, which is projected to reach $50 billion. The government has also significantly increased the NDIS agency's workforce by nearly 2,000 employees to improve service delivery, while some parliamentarians and advocates raise concerns about potential impacts on participant rights and funding.

Full Text:
Mr Edershang.
Thank you, President. Westerners waiting for public transport improvements rejoice, for there are extra Sunday train services from Laverton to Altona. Imagine travelling along a scenic return journey through Melbourne's inner west and along Port Phillip Bay at Altona. Alas, last Sunday was the last day when Western residents could experience a time when public transport was a source of pride and a well-run metropolis was judged on its regular train services. Steam Rail Victoria ran a series of one-way steam locomotive trips with return shuttles on a schedule that would make a local commuter weep. Nostalgia is delightful but gives cold comfort to those parts of the West so so lacking in public transport options. Similarly, the government's announcement of free public transport is poor consolation for the same reasons. What's the benefit of travelling free on public transport if it doesn't exist in the first place? We know that buses are the cheapest, easiest and most flexible option for addressing the gaps in our transport infrastructure. And Victoria's bus plan, released by then Transport Minister Ben Carroll back in 2023, recognised that too. The key objective of the 2023 bus plan was to work with industry to develop a bus reform implementation plan to transform the bus network and align it to meet growing demand. Splendid. Ambitious. The sort of aspiration we'd expect from a Labor government. Well, sadly, Victoria's bus plan was rejected by Cabinet in 2023. This was particularly disastrous for the Outer West, one of the fastest-growing regions in Australia, which is still left with a patchwork of badly underserviced public transport deserts. People need accessible, cheap transport. We are in the midst of a fuel crisis that won't be resolved any time soon. Families in the outer west deprived of accessible public transport and thus already spending a fortune on petrol will have no choice but to absorb the fuel hikes. Meanwhile, communities in wealthier, leafier suburbs well serviced by public transport will reap the benefits of this taxpayer-funded public transport logistics. Now, more than ever, we need a bus plan. So the action I am seeking is that the Minister for Public Transport provides an update on when the government intends to release a revised bus reform implementation plan to provide some public transport relief to the outer western suburbs. Thank you.

The bill creates a regulatory regime to ensure Australian activities are undertaken consistent with this new treaty. This includes regulating the collection and use of marine genetic resources from areas beyond national jurisdiction and provides a framework for Australia to recognise area-based management tools established by the treaty, such as marine protected areas. Australia has engaged in the more than 20 years of discussion and negotiations for this treaty and we are co-chairing the process to prepare for the first meeting of the Conference of the the Parties. I thank all members for their contribution and I commend the bill.

Thank you Deputy Speaker. I present the revised explanatory memorandum to this bill and I move that this bill be now read a second time. Thank you. The Albanese Labor Government is committed to ensuring the NDIS is a pillar pillar of Australia's unique social safety net. That means that we are committed to ensuring the National Disability Insurance Scheme provides essential disability support for people with permanent and significant disability today and into the future. We are committed to an NDIS that is fair, consistent and empowering for people with permanent and significant disability. An NDIS that is sustainable, effective, safe and operates with integrity. This government has been committed to taking fraud and misconduct in the NDIS seriously. Those who defraud the NDIS are exploiting the hundreds of thousands of Australians who rely on the life-changing support the NDIS delivers. We were left with a mess in coming to government. Under the former Coalition Government, the NDIS was a soft target. Our government acted quickly, investing over $550 million in tackling fraud and non-compliance, setting up the Fraud Fusion Taskforce and passing Getting the NDIS Back on Track Act 1 to place it on a sustainable footing. But there is more work to do and this bill is an important step. Today I introduce the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment Integrity and Safeguarding Bill to the House. This legislation will ensure that the NDIS remains true to its purpose, safe, strong and centred on the people it serves. We cannot ignore the findings of the Royal Commission into violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation of people with disability. The stories were harrowing. They revealed a system that was fractured, under-resourced and too often blind to harm. Australians with disability told us in no uncertain terms the days of abuse and neglect must end. The findings of the independent review into the NDIS reinforced this call. The review told us the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission must be more responsive, more powerful and more trusted. It told us that regulatory gaps are putting lives at risk. It told us that without reform the integrity of the scheme and the safety of its participants cannot be guaranteed. That is unacceptable. This government will not stand by. This bill delivers on our commitment to reform the NDIS It does three things. First is strengthen safeguards. We are giving the NDIS Commission the powers it needs to protect participants. That means tougher penalties, up to $16 million for corporations that breach the law and prison terms for those who recklessly or deliberately put lives at risk. It means expanding banning orders to capture not just providers and workers but auditors and consultants who compromise safety. And it means introducing anti-promotion powers to stop unethical advertising because the NDIS is not a marketplace for exploitation. Second, it improves integrity and responsiveness. We are tightening compliance requirements so the NDIS Commission can act swiftly when harm is suspected. And we are introducing evidentiary certificates to streamline enforcement because justice delayed is justice denied. denied. Third, it modernises the scheme. Electronic claim forms will replace outdated processes, saving time and reducing fraud. A 90-day cooling-off period will protect participants who choose to leave the scheme, ensuring decisions are made with care. This bill, as amended by the Senate, also introduces whistleblower protections that will support those in the NDIS who see something to say something. These reforms were not written in isolation. They were shaped by the voices of participants, their families, carers, providers and states. We held forums across the country, online and in person, because this scheme belongs to the people it serves. And what did we hear? We heard that accountability matters. We heard that penalties must be strong enough to deter harm. We heard that predatory behaviour must be stamped out. We listened and now we are acting. The vast majority of providers do the right thing. They deliver safe, quality services that change lives. This bill is not about them. It is about the minority, those who recklessly or intentionally cause harm, exploit or defraud people with disability. To them, I say, you don't belong in the NDIS Importantly, it is also about people with disabilities and their families. To them, I say unequivocally that your wellbeing, your dignity and your life is just as valued as any other Australian. I commend this bill to the House.
I thank the Minister. The question is that this bill be now read a second time. Is leave granted for to continue the debate? Leave is granted. Thank you. I call the Member for Lindsay.
Thank you Mr Deputy Speaker. Every day thousands of Australian families rely on the NDIS For Australians living with significant and permanent disability, it provides not just support but opportunity. It is a therapy session that can change a child's trajectory. It is a support that keeps a loved one safe at home. The difference between coping and not. For these families, the NDIS is not a line item in a budget. It is deeply personal. It is what holds their world together. It is a lifeline. It is the difference between a life of isolation and a life of choice. That is exactly why why the Coalition's support for the NDIS remains steadfast. We understand that the NDIS is about more than service delivery. It is is about dignity, independence and the right to choose. It is one of the most significant reforms in our nation's history but the NDIS is now at a crossroads. Built to support around 410,000 people, it is now supporting more than 760,000. This growth raises a serious question. How do we ensure the system keeps pace without falling over? For the NDIS to continue delivering support, it must be sustainable.

Headline: Melbourne girl, 13, allegedly shouted antisemitic remarks, threw eggs and swerved car towards Jewish families
Full Text:
Jewish families 'narrowly escaped being struck by the car' after girl swerved towards them in Ripponlea, police say

    A 13-year-old Melbourne girl has been charged with 52 offences including allegedly shouting antisemitic remarks, throwing eggs and swerving a stolen car towards members of the Jewish community.

    

    Victorian police said in a statement on Tuesday that the girl and two other girls were alleged to have been seen driving the stolen black Hyundai sedan in the south-eastern suburbs of Hampton, Ripponlea and Caulfield over multiple days last week.

    

    Police alleged that on 25 March, the girls shouted "offensive, antisemitic remarks" and threw eggs at pedestrians.

    

    Three days later, the car, allegedly driven by the 13-year-old, swerved towards Jewish families in Ripponlea about 7pm, police said, as the group crossed the road at the intersection of Hotham Street and Glen Eira Road.

    

    They "narrowly escaped being struck by the car", police said.

    

    "There were no physical injuries and the car, which was allegedly stolen from a gym in Caulfield, fled the scene.

    

    "Police will allege the driver, a 13-year-old girl from the Bayside area, was also involved in several other incidents involving erratic driving in stolen cars."

    

    On Monday night, police responded to an alleged hit-and-run in Brighton.

    

    It is alleged a male cyclist was travelling along St Kilda Street when an occupant of a stolen silver SUV attempted to hit the bike with the passenger door about 6.50pm.

    

    The driver of the SUV then allegedly crashed into the rear of the bike.

    

    The cyclist, a 45-year-old Brighton man, was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, police said, and the driver fled the scene.

    

    Just after midnight on Tuesday morning, police said teenagers travelling in a stolen white Volkswagen Golf rammed an e-scooter with two people on board in Elwood.

    

    "Both riders fell from the e-scooter as it crashed into a parked vehicle. They did not require medical attention," police said.

    

    "One of the victims and a passerby began filming the offending vehicle, before one of the teenagers allegedly threatened them."

    

    Police spotted the van that was allegedly involved in the crash a short time later.

    

    Police said the driver allegedly travelled across a footpath and "took off at speed" on the Nepean Highway, before travelling on the Dingley Bypass, the EastLink, Princes Highway and the Monash Freeway.

    

    "Police successfully deployed stop sticks on Dandenong Road in East Malvern, before the car came to a stop on Waverley Road," police said.

    

    "The three female occupants were arrested at the scene and taken into custody."

    

    The 13-year-old girl from the Bayside area was charged with 52 offences including reckless conduct endangering serious injury, multiple counts of theft, multiple counts of theft of motor vehicle, burglary, handling stolen goods and "threatening physical harm or property damage on ground of a protected attribute".

    

    She was remanded to appear at a children's court.

    

    Another 13-year-old girl and a 16-year-old girl, both from the Cardinia area, were also arrested.

    

    They were charged with theft of motor vehicle and handling stolen goods and were bailed to appear at a children's court at a later date.

    

    "Investigations into the series of incidents remains ongoing," police said.

    

    "There is absolutely no place at all in our society for hate-based behaviour and such activity will not be tolerated."

    A biker is fighting for life after a horror crash shut down a key section of a major Victorian highway, sparking traffic chaos.

    The freeway is currently closed to outbound traffic between Heatherton Rd and Belgrave-Hallam Rd, with motorists being diverted through Dandenong South.

    

    A Victoria Police spokesman said: "Emergency services responded to a collision in Endeavour Hills on Tuesday.

    

    "It is believed two cars and a motorcycle collided on the Monash Freeway near Heatherton Rd just after 3.30pm.

    "The drivers of the cars were not injured and stopped at the scene to assist. The exact cause of the collision is being investigated."

    The spokesman said: "Ambulance Victoria was called to an incident in the Endeavour Hills at around 2.50pm today."

    

    "A specialist air ambulance helicopter crew, advanced life support and mobile intensive care ambulance paramedic crews attended the scene.

And there are two cases in the US that have had big fines against these companies. And Australia is really taking it to them. And that's something that all Australians should be proud of.
The government, as you heard there in question, time says that the law will be upheld. They'll throw the book at them. Will that happen?
Well, this is a test for the Minister. was very happy to fly halfway around the world over $100,000 of taxpayer money to deliver an eight-minute speech talking about how great these laws were. Well, a law is only as good as its effectiveness and its impact in the community, and it is not... Sorry, the eSafety Commissioner has a a role to play, absolutely, but ultimate responsibility sits with the minister. Happy to get up and claim a lot of credit. Now the minister needs to deliver for Australian people. I talk to young people in my community all the time and they're still on these social media platforms and say there's a lot of ways that they can get around it. So the social media companies have to be held to account, but that sits with the minister to deliver for the Australian people.
OK, so do you think the laws are strong enough?
Well, that's what we're going to see. We're going to see whether the laws and the penalties are strong enough, because it looks like from the evidence given today and from the conversation many politicians, myself included, are having with the community that it's not working. So announcing something is great. Delivering on it is ultimately what a minister has to do. And this this minister hasn't delivered so far.
Do the laws need to be even tighter then? Well, I think this minister is delivering. That's the whole point. Now we know with this compliance report what is is happening, what companies aren't complying. So this is the laws working because now the eSafety Commissioner with the minister, they can take these companies to court and they can say, if you don't comply, you're going to face up to $50 million in fines. Surely that's the law's working. Okay. Do you think they care that much about $50 million? They make a lot of money.
So we're about to find out. It's not the law's working. It's actually an admission of failure by the Minister, respectfully, Sally. The law's working would be the Minister standing up today, as she would have hoped to have done, to say it is a success. These accounts have been shut down. Young people are off social media. That was what the Minister wanted to do.
But she wasn't able to because they're not respecting... it, though. Like, let me just... That's my point. But isn't that on them? Well, no, it's on them. No, but at the end of the day, it's on the minister because the government sets the law, the government enforces the law. Yeah, but if I break the law, right, like drink driving is illegal in Victoria, where I live.
Sorry, I'm just setting up the whole thing. Is it the Minister for Transport or Police's responsibility that I drink, drug, throw? It's both. So the social media companies absolutely should abide by the law and the books should be thrown at them. That is their responsibility. But it is any minister's responsibility to ensure the law is enforced. To use your example, there has to be police on the road catching drink drivers. If there's no consequence, people won't follow the law. And that sits with the minister. I'm not letting the social media giants off the hook. They absolutely should comply and the books should be thrown at them if they're not following the law. Absolutely. That point, there is some merit in the point about the compliance regime. This is the big test for it. Sure, absolutely. And if we can't see an outcome and some really tangible changes, doesn't it show that the laws are actually not working? So, let's be clear. We are the world-leading country on this. We are the first in the world to do this. So, Australians should be proud that we are policy entrepreneurs. As an idea, but the execution is the different matters. let's talk about execution as well, because millions and millions of accounts have already been deactivated or people have been restricted.
Young people have been restricted. So yes, there have been some people who have been able to circumvent, but there have also been young people who haven't been able to get through. And we've made a significant cultural change as well because no longer are parents having to battle their kids to say, don't get on social media. Now it's the law in this country. That conversation has changed. I know it's changed in my household. I say, the Prime Minister said you can't be on YouTube, and my son, he respects that.
Yeah, I think some kids are definitely biting by it, others are not, and I think that's the story of life, right? I want to move on to another topic, which is the size of the parliament. Your side of politics today, Angus Taylor, Matt Canavan, the new Nationals leader, stood up, made this an issue. It's not really... I don't know. No, I've been receiving correspondence about it. Have you? Yeah, people are... You know, the government have put it on the agenda. Don Farrell spoke about it. They've clearly given orders to one of the committees, the Electoral Matters Committee, to look at the size of parliament. And we're saying that any time of crisis, this government shouldn't be focused on adding more politicians and more cost to the system. We should be doing the job that we've been elected to do and focus on that.
Prime Minister made a point before I come to you, which was, you know, I don't really need to game any system which you've accused them of. They've got 94 seats.
He's always looking for an angle, this Prime Minister.
But it resonated because they have a lot of seats.
But he didn't rule it out. He didn't explicitly say we would not be expanding the parliament. And we've heard before from this Prime Minister, he uses tricky words, like I have no plans at this time, and he used those tricky words again today. So it is a concern that people have been raising. Well, no.
Sorry. I know, but I'm very fair about the facts. Don Farrell has put it on the table. There's no bill before parliament. No, there's not a bill yet, but there's a consideration of it. This is being discussed in a parliamentary committee which the opposition are part of. Have those discussions there. But at the moment, we are focused on getting fuel in the country, getting the prices down. We are not focused on... Sally, you've become very good at avoiding my questions, which is very impressive, so I'll ask you again. Go ahead, Give me a best shot. What's the idea of expanding the number of politicians? I love what we have now. I think it is a great size. We're representing our community as well. I even think Aaron is doing a semi-decent job.
You almost gave me a compliment there. You just endorsed him as the the candidate again at the next election? Yeah, alright, I will.
Alright, I'm sure the Liberal Party will be playing those ads at the next election.
No, but, okay, so you think it's about right that you can't see the case for change? I think it's about right. I'm really happy to represent my electorate, 120,000 people, and we're doing everything we can to be supporting the good people of Reid. I heard in Angus Taylor's comments today, you know, whether you think it's too expensive or not, you can think that, but there was also really an anti-politician vibe to it, and it struck me that these two men were politicians and that this whole kind of getting on the bandwagon of hating politicians is not very helpful to our democracy, is it?
When public trust in politics has eroded, when our institutions are under pressure, why are you helping? No, we're legitimately putting a case forward that, as Sally said, the size of parliament is the right size now and we should use every taxpayer dollar well. We last term had our staff expanded to make sure that we could service our communities to the best of our ability. And same as Sally, I love representing the seat of Casey and getting out and meeting as many people as possible. But we need to recognise that more politicians is not the answer, and that's what we're doing. We're echoing the concerns that have been raised with us.
Do you get the point I'm making, though, that sort of, you know, railing against politicians when you're a politician seems a bit weird?
Oh, I understand that... Get my point, right?
I get your point, I get your point. People are... You know, there is a level of frustration with politics and the political system that we need to acknowledge and we need to focus on working hard every day, engaging with our communities, putting forward policies that are going to solve the challenges that our communities face and the country faces, and that's what we should be focused on. That's why the Coalition led the way by proposing and writing to the Prime Minister requesting the fuel excise cut, because we were hearing from our communities that they were under pressure. It was great to see that the Prime Minister imitation, greatest form of flattery, followed us and announced that move on Monday. So that's what we're focused on. OK, we've only got 30 seconds, but, yes, you did do it. Were you following the Coalition? I don't think we have to be who said it first, who said it when. What people want is for us to come together as a country, different levels of government, different sides of politics, to work through what has been a very challenging period. Yeah, it really has. It has been a difficult period. Well, I wish you both a happy Easter, or break if if don't quite do Easter. Thank you very much. Thank you.

Headline: Dumping epidemic
Full Text:
RESIDENTS' anger is growing after two major illegal dumping incidents, both believed to involve truckloads of waste, were discovered within days of each other at a Wallan freeway exit ramp and at Lightwood Crossing in Wandong.

    The latest incidents have again highlighted the Mitchell Shire's growing battle with largescale dumping, with locals describing the scenes as "disgraceful" and "completely brazen".

    The first dumping was discovered at the freeway exit ramp in Wallan, where a substantial pile of rubbish, believed to have been offloaded from a truck, was left dangerously close to traffic.

    Residents say the location is particularly concerning given the high-speed environment, with debris posing a potential hazard for drivers entering and exiting the freeway.

    The incident comes as major road works continue in the area, including upgrades to the Watson Street interchange, which are already creating changed traffic conditions and increased congestion.

    A second, similar incident was uncovered at Lightwood Crossing in Wandong, where another large load of waste was dumped in a semi-rural setting.

    The scale of the dumping has led residents to believe it was carried out by a commercial operator rather than an individual, with materials reportedly including mixed household and construction waste.

    The incidents have reignited frustration across the community, with many residents questioning how offenders continue to operate without being caught.

    Illegal dumping is not new to the area. In February, residents and council were left to clean up another significant dump on Wallan Heights Road, with authorities warning that ratepayers ultimately foot the bill.

    Council leaders have repeatedly stressed that dumping is unlawful and costly, with cleanups often requiring significant resources and specialist disposal.

    Residents are now calling for stronger penalties and more visible enforcement, arguing that repeat incidents show current deterrents are not working.

    "There's no way this is just someone with a trailer. This is organised dumping, and it keeps happening," one local said.

    With two major incidents in quick succession, the message from the community is clear: enough is enough.

    Both sites are expected to require significant clean-up efforts, with costs likely to fall to council unless those responsible can be identified.

    Authorities are urging anyone with information, dashcam footage, or who witnessed suspicious activity in either location to come forward.

    To report, phone the Mitchell Shire Council Local Laws Department on 5734 6200, or use the "My Mitchell" mobile app. Alternatively, visit www.mitchellshire.vic.gov.au and report via the contact form, or email mitchell@mitchellshire.vicgou.au

Interview
Stolen wages and cases of modern slavery by Australian employers have been revealed in a a national programme aimed to protect migrant workers. In New South Wales alone, more than a million dollars in potential... have been revealed in a national programme aimed to protect migrant workers.
In New South Wales alone, more than a million dollars in potential unpaid wage claims have been identified, while in Victoria, more than $230,000 has already been recovered. The programme set up by the Department of Home Affairs could be at risk of being cut in the federal budget. Reporter Isabel Rose says the programme was initially set up to teach migrant workers about their workplace rights.
It's something that was set up by the federal government a year ago, which was meant to teach migrant workers who'd come to Australia about the sort of rights they have here in the workplace. $13.5 million was put aside, being run by the Home Affairs Department, and it's been running sessions across the country in every state, run by unions mostly, and it's been speaking to hundreds, thousands of workers who have raised some of these concerns. Just as an example, 16,400 visa holders have been spoken to. In Victoria, $200,000 has been clawed back for workers in unpaid wages. The number is a lot higher in New South Wales It's about $1.35 million in unpaid wages. In Queensland, for example, the programme discovered there were 70 African migrants who were working on this farm in Gatton who were not paid their superannuation for their entire period of employment. When the union picked that up, the business phoenixed because they were trying to get out of paying it. So there have been several cases of exploitation that have been picked up as as part of this programme
And you've spoken to people who've been exploited at work. What have they told you?
Well, one of the women I've spoken to's name is Viviana. She is a Colombian national. She is a clinical psychologist in Colombia and she came to Australia thinking she would have some better work opportunities. She took a job as a worker for a contractor for the National Disability Insurance Scheme relies heavily on migrants in this country, and she found that she was harassed at all hours of the day during her work. She was called at 1am and 2am by her boss on her days off. was called at 1am and 2am by her boss on her days off. When she raised this issue with her boss, she was eventually fired and $40,000 of her wages were withheld. It's caused her an immense amount of stress. This is what she had to tell me. I didn't have too much options in this time. Like, I didn't know... I didn't have support, to be honest. I didn't know here. I didn't have, like, emotional support. I didn't have money.
So Viviana was about to leave Australia and essentially give up when she said she happened to see a Facebook post written in Spanish, which was her first language. She was able to actually understand that how she was being treated was illegal in this country. She was able to speak to Unions New South Wales and they were able to help her get her money back.
Unions New South Wales though, says it believes that funding is about to be cut for this programme How come?
Well, as the government looks through its books ahead of the May budget, it's really trying to make savings. And the union says its staff have been told, essentially, that they shouldn't expect ongoing funding for this programme They were given $13.5 million for a year. They're looking for three more years' funding. But at this stage, they say it's not guaranteed. And the Home Affairs Department, when I asked them, have declined to comment to the ABC

Full Text:
negative gearing and capital gains tax discount were introduced as paired concessions over 20 years ago, house prices have risen at twice the rate of wages. Sydney is now the second least affordable city in the world. Young Australians are working hard, saving what they can, paying down large HECS debts and living at home for longer. Yet the deposit required keeps racing ahead. For many, it has become a Sisyphean task. Negative gearing is also failing to deliver new housing supply, with seven out of eight investment loans going towards established properties. Tax-advantaged investors are simply outbidding first-home buyers. As more Australians recognise that our housing tax settings are fuelling intergenerational inequity, the appetite for reform is growing. So, with the government considering housing taxation changes ahead of the May budget, I want to highlight recent evidence from polling, surveys, submissions and a local deliberative democracy conference that show clear and strong support for reform within my electorate of McKellar. In June 2024 I hosted the Mackellar People's Jury on Housing in partnership with the New Democracy. 29 randomly selected Mackellar residents heard from a broad range of housing experts then they deliberated on their top policy recommendations. Prior to the day, we received 79 detailed submissions from McKellar locals, which informed the jury's deliberations. The top recommendation agreed upon by 28 of the 29 jurors was for review and reform of Australia's housing taxation settings. I also conducted an online survey of people living in McKellar. Of the 3,143 local respondents, a majority 65% supported changing the capital gains tax discount, with only 27% opposed to changing it. Lastly, polling by YouGov released just this week again backs this up with figures showing 62% of people in McKellar supporting housing tax reform. So the message is clear. Australians want a fair go restored and this must include fairer housing tax settings.
I call the member for Tangi. Thank you, Madam Speaker. More than 28% of people in Tangi speak a language other than English at home. The top 10 languages used in home in Tangi included Mandarin, Cantonese, Indonesian, Tamil, Punjabi, Malayanam, Korean, Hindi, Italian, and Arabic. The languages of my childhood included Mandarin, Teochew, Hokkien, and Malay. But being multi-language has actually provided me with lots of opportunity to connect with so many people. Language has shaped who I am. I want to praise the 13 community language schools in Tangny that teach languages such as Punjabi, Tamil, Arabic and also Hungarian. These schools have received the the federal government's community language school grants to help strengthen their ability to help young Australians learn a language other than English. Alberta Primary School is a public Chinese-English bilingual school in Tangney. The school has a commitment to languages that is unmatched in the whole of Tangney. Fifteen years ago, Alberta Primary School Principal Tim Bermel, he researched a bilingual bilingual programme in Melbourne and spent a lot of time with researchers learning about the advantages of bilingual brain. I will encourage our community, young or old, to learn a language. In a few languages, I would like to say thank you. I call the Member for Mallee.
Well said, I've got to say. Deputy Speaker, Labour's fuel supply crisis is undermining road safety, local government services and community life in regional Australia. In Kenaiva, Garoak and Edenhope, in the southwest of my electorate of Mallee, on the Victoria and South Australian border, the West Wimmera Shire Council can no longer afford basic road maintenance. Bitumen is too expensive, communities are cutting back on essential travel and regional Australians are being left behind, despite the Prime Minister's promise to the contrary. Liquid fuels do not just power cars and farm machinery. They account for nearly half of Australia's total energy demand and is essential to farms, productivity, construction materials and critically, bitumen. When fuel prices surge and supply tightens, the damage spreads quickly and deeply through the economy. Australia imports 80 to 90% of its liquid fuel. When costs rise, regional communities, already at the end of their long supply chains, are hit hardest and fastest. David, the CEO of West Wimmera Shire, has made it clear to me. Skyrocketing fuel and bitumen bitumen costs are forcing Council to defer desperately needed road maintenance. Bitumen prices have surged as much as 35 to 40 per cent, creating a road safety crisis. Regional councils are already financially stressed and in Victoria the condition of regional roads is frankly indefensible. Potholes stretch as far as the eye can see. Delaying repairs increases risk, putting motorists, freight operators, emergency vehicles and school buses, and therefore human lives, in danger every single day. Regional Australians should not be asked to accept unsafe roads because local governments cannot afford the fuel and materials required to fix them. Yet that is exactly what is happening. And the fallout does not stop with council services. In West Wimbera, people live vast distances from essential services. There is no free public transport, thank you to the Premier Rising fuel costs and a lack of fuel are forcing pensioners, volunteers and families to make impossible choices. Leanne from Kenaiva told me I have had to cancel medical appointment because I can't get diesel from our local roadhouse for tests that can only be done in Horsham. She was referring to medical care. West Woomera Shire Council has told me that people across their region are pulling back from community sport and stepping away from volunteering roles.
We're not just talking about housing, Labor is building it. I'm thrilled that works have commenced in Swan, 171 new affordable apartments in Rivervale. This isn't just a construction update, this is real tangible change for people in our community and I want to take a moment to talk about who those people are because behind every one of these 171 homes is a story that deserves to be told. Think about the nurse who finishes a double shift at 2am and faces a long commute home because she simply cannot afford to live close to the hospital where she works. Think about the veteran who served our country with honour and dedication and now struggles to find stable and affordable place to call home. These are the people that these homes are for. These are people who served our community and they deserve to live in the community where they live and work and we would love to call them our neighbours.

Well, it's something that was set up by the federal government a year ago, which was meant to teach migrant workers who'd come to Australia about the sort of rights that they have here in the workplace. $13.5 million was put put aside, being run by the Home Affairs Department, and it's been running sessions across the country in every state, run by unions mostly, and it's been been speaking to hundreds, thousands of workers who have raised some of these concerns.
